5.title: The Qualifications of the Perfect Priest
5.overview:
Chapter 5 introduces the great theme of Hebrews’ central section: the priesthood of Jesus after the order of Melchizedek. The writer begins with careful pastoral method, first establishing what all genuine high priests have in common — chosen from men, appointed to represent men before God, able to deal gently with the weak, called by God rather than self-appointed — and then applying each criterion to Jesus. The application is astonishing at every point: Jesus meets every genuine qualification, while transcending the one fatal limitation that disqualified all the Levitical priests: the need to offer for their own sins. He had no sin of his own. His offering was entirely, unreservedly, and permanently for others.

The quotation of Psalm 110:4 in verse 6 — “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek” — opens a new front in the argument that will occupy the writer through chapter 7. This single verse from the Psalms, spoken long after the Levitical system was established, implies that the Levitical system was never the final word on priesthood. There was a more ancient, more mysterious, more permanent order: the order of Melchizedek.

The chapter closes with one of the most tender passages in the letter (vv. 7–9): a description of Jesus in Gethsemane, offering prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears, heard because of his reverence, learning obedience through suffering, and thereby being made perfect as the source of eternal salvation. Then, without warning, the third warning passage begins (5:11–6:20) — a pastoral rebuke of the congregation’s spiritual sluggishness. They have remained on milk when they should be eating solid food. The most demanding section of the letter is coming, and they need to be ready for it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Every high priest is chosen from among men and appointed to act on their behalf toward God, offering gifts and sacrifices for sins (v.1); he can deal gently with the ignorant and wayward because he is himself beset with weakness (v.2), and must therefore offer sacrifice for his own sins as well as the people’s (v.3). And no one takes the honour for himself, but only when called by God, as Aaron was (v.4).

So Christ did not exalt himself, but was appointed by the one who said “You are my Son, today I have begotten you” (v.5), and elsewhere “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek” (v.6). In the days of his flesh he offered prayers with loud cries and tears to the one able to save him from death, and was heard for his reverence (v.7); though a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered (v.8); and being made perfect he became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him (v.9), designated by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek (v.10).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Qualification That Is Also the Flaw

Verse 2 names the rarest pastoral quality in one word. Metriopathein means to moderate one’s feelings, to take the middle path between two failures: a priest must not be indifferent to sin and must not be enraged by it, and both extremes disqualify a man for the work. What makes the gentleness possible is that he is “beset” with weakness — the verb means surrounded by it, wearing it like a garment. A man who knows his own frailty from inside cannot be contemptuous of anyone else’s.

And then verse 3 names the cost. The very thing that makes the human priest sympathetic makes him compromised: on the Day of Atonement he had to deal with himself before he could deal with anybody. That is precisely the gap Christ fills — sympathy without the compromise (4:15).

Psalm 110:4 at verse 6 is the hinge of the whole letter. Here is a psalm universally read as messianic in which God swears the coming king will be a priest — constitutionally impossible, since kings came from Judah and priests from Levi and the lines never crossed. Unless the priesthood is not Levitical. Two words carry it: forever, which no Levite could be because they died; and after the order of, a line older than Levi and independent of him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verse 4 had a sharp contemporary edge. Scripture guards the boundary severely — Korah was swallowed for arguing the priesthood should be open (Num 16), Uzziah came out of the temple a leper (2 Chr 26:16–21), Saul lost a kingdom for offering a sacrifice himself (1 Sam 13). And in the readers’ own day the high priesthood had become notoriously political: Rome appointed and deposed high priests, and the office was traded within a few powerful families. A congregation tempted back toward the temple was being tempted toward a priesthood that had plainly taken the honour for itself.

Now: Verse 7 is one of the most startling verses in the New Testament, and it should not be hurried. No Gospel records Jesus weeping in Gethsemane; the writer says there were loud cries — the word for a shout, not a murmur — and tears. Then the difficulty every reader feels: he was heard, and he died. The Greek can mean saved out of death rather than from dying, brought through rather than spared, which fits a prayer that ended “nevertheless not my will”. So the Son of God prayed with shouting and tears, did not receive what he asked in the form he asked it, and was heard. Unanswered prayer, in the shape most people mean by the phrase, is not evidence of being unheard.

And “he learned obedience” cannot mean he moved from disobedience — he learned it by experience, which is the difference between a man who has always intended to be loyal and the same man after loyalty has cost him something.

verseByVerse.quote: For every high priest chosen from among men is appointed to act on behalf of men in relation to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. He can deal gently with the ignorant and wayward, since he himself is beset with weakness. Because of this he is obligated to offer sacrifice for his own sins just as he does for those of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having called Jesus a great high priest, the writer now sets out what a high priest is. Three qualifications are given here and a fourth in verse 4, and the argument of the next several chapters depends on them.

First, he is “chosen from among men”. He must be one of the people he represents. That is not a detail; a representative who does not share the condition of those he stands for cannot stand for them, and it is why chapter 2 insisted that the Son had to be made like his brothers in every respect.

Second, he is “appointed to act on behalf of men in relation to God”. The direction is upward. A prophet faces the people with a word from God; a priest faces God with people on his hands. His whole business is Godward, and its content is stated: “to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.”

Third, and this is the one the writer dwells on, “he can deal gently with the ignorant and wayward, since he himself is beset with weakness.”

The word for dealing gently is metriopathein, and it is precise: to moderate one’s feelings, to take the middle path between two failures. A priest must not be indifferent to sin, and he must not be enraged by it. Both extremes disqualify a man for the work. Anyone who has been to a minister with something shameful knows how rare the middle way is.

And note who he deals gently with: “the ignorant and wayward” — those who sin without knowing and those who wander off. Not the defiant. The old covenant made no provision for the high-handed sin (Num 15:30), and the writer keeps that boundary in view; it will surface again at 10:26.

What makes the gentleness possible is stated flatly: “since he himself is beset with weakness.” The verb means to be surrounded by, to have it wrapped around him like a garment. A man who knows his own frailty from the inside cannot be contemptuous of anyone else’s.

And then verse 3 states the cost of that qualification, which is also its flaw: “he is obligated to offer sacrifice for his own sins just as he does for those of the people.” The very thing that makes him sympathetic makes him compromised. On the Day of Atonement the high priest had to deal with himself before he could deal with anybody else — and that is the gap Christ fills.

verseByVerse.quote: And no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And no one takes this honour for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was.” The fourth qualification, and it is about appointment.

The priesthood is not a career. It cannot be applied for, earned by merit, or seized by the ambitious. It is given — and Aaron is named because his call was public, unmistakable, and not of his own seeking. He was, if anything, a reluctant figure who had already made a golden calf.

Scripture keeps this boundary with some severity. Korah and his company argued that the whole congregation was holy and the priesthood should be open, and the ground swallowed them (Num 16). King Uzziah, a good king, went into the temple to burn incense and came out a leper (2 Chr 26:16–21). Saul offered the sacrifice himself when Samuel was late, and lost his kingdom for it (1 Sam 13:8–14).

The severity is not arbitrary. If a man could appoint himself to represent others before God, then access to God would ultimately rest on human initiative — and everyone approaching would be depending on somebody’s self-assessment.

There is also an immediate relevance here that the first readers would have felt. The high priesthood in their own day had become notoriously political: Rome appointed and deposed high priests, and the office had been bought and traded within a few powerful families. A congregation being tempted back toward the temple system was being tempted toward a priesthood that had plainly taken the honour for itself.

And the verse sets up the argument that follows. If no one may take the honour, then Christ’s priesthood must rest on a divine appointment, and the writer is about to produce the two texts in which God makes it — which is exactly what verses 5 and 6 do.

verseByVerse.quote: So also Christ did not exalt himself to be made a high priest, but was appointed by him who said to him, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you”; as he says also in another place, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
“So also Christ did not exalt himself to be made a high priest.” The qualification of verse 4 is met, and it is met by the one person who could have claimed the office on his own account.

Pause on. The Son through whom the world was made did not appoint himself to anything. He waited to be given it — which is the same disposition Philippians describes when it says he did not count equality with God a thing to be exploited.

Then two quotations, and they are the two halves of the appointment.

The first is Psalm 2:7, already used at 1:5: “You are my Son, today I have begotten you.” It establishes the relationship. Before there is any question of office, there is sonship.

The second is Psalm 110:4, and it is the verse this letter will spend three chapters on: “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”

Psalm 110 has already been quoted at 1:13 for its first verse, where the Lord tells David’s Lord to sit at his right hand. Now the writer takes its fourth verse, and it is the hinge of the entire letter. Here is a psalm, universally read as messianic, in which God swears that the coming king will be a priest — which was constitutionally impossible, since kings came from Judah and priests from Levi, and the two lines never crossed.

Unless the priesthood in question is not Levitical. Hence Melchizedek, a figure who appears in three verses of Genesis and is never mentioned again in the Old Testament except in this one psalm.

Two words carry the weight. “Forever” — which no Levitical priest could be, since they died. And “after the order of” — a different line entirely, older than Levi and independent of him.

The writer names it here and then does something remarkable: he stops, and does not return to Melchizedek until 7:1. What comes between is a rebuke and a warning, because he has judged that his readers are in no condition to take the argument in.

verseByVerse.quote: In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“In the days of his flesh.” The phrase sets a period — the years when the Son lived under the conditions we live under, which are over now.

“Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears.” This is one of the most startling verses in the New Testament, and resist the temptation to hurry past it.

None of the Gospels records Jesus weeping in Gethsemane. Luke mentions sweat like drops of blood; Mark says he was greatly distressed and troubled. The writer of Hebrews knows something about that night that the Gospels do not tell us, or he is drawing out what they imply. Either way, he says there were loud cries — the word is used of a shout, not a murmur — and there were tears.

“To him who was able to save him from death.” Note the precision. God was able. The prayer was not addressed into a void or to a power that could not manage it.

“And he was heard because of his reverence.”

Here is the difficulty every reader feels: he was heard, and he died. What does it mean that the prayer was answered?

The Greek can mean saved out of death rather than from dying — brought through it rather than spared it. That fits the facts and it fits Gethsemane, where the prayer itself was conditional: if it be possible, let this cup pass; nevertheless not my will but yours. A prayer that ends “nevertheless” is answered when the Father’s will is done, and it was.

The word for “reverence” means godly fear, a holy caution — the disposition of a son who wants above everything not to displease. He was heard because of that, not because of the volume of the crying.

And consider what this verse gives to a praying person. The Son of God prayed with shouting and tears, and did not get what he asked for in the form he asked for it, and was heard. Unanswered prayer, in the shape most people mean by the phrase, is not evidence of being unheard.

verseByVerse.quote: Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered. And being made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him, being designated by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered.” The Greek is a piece of wordplay — emathen, he learned, and epathen, he suffered. Learning and suffering rhyme, and the proverb was familiar in Greek.

“Although he was a son” concedes the objection before it is raised. We would expect sonship to exempt him. It did not; if anything it was the reason.

“He learned obedience” needs care, because it cannot mean he moved from disobedience to obedience. He was always perfectly willing. What he learned was obedience by experience — the difference between a man who has always intended to be loyal and the same man after loyalty has cost him something. He knew what obedience was; in the garden he came to know what it weighs.

“And being made perfect” — the same word as 2:10, brought to completion, made fully fit for an office. Not moral improvement. Qualification.

“He became the source of eternal salvation.” The word for source is the word for cause — he is not a means to it or a condition of it but its origin. And note eternal, which in this letter is always set against the temporary: an annually repeated sacrifice produced an annually repeated forgiveness.

“To all who obey him.” It is a striking way to describe Christians — not those who believe, which is what we might expect, but those who obey. The two are not alternatives in this letter; the wilderness generation’s failure was called unbelief in one verse and disobedience in the next (3:19; 4:6). Faith that does not eventually move the feet was never the thing Hebrews means by faith.

And there is a symmetry here that the writer has arranged deliberately. He learned obedience through suffering; he became the source of salvation to those who obey. The pattern the Son walked is the pattern his people walk.

“Being designated by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek.” The name returns, closing the paragraph — and the writer is now ready to explain it, except that he has looked at his congregation and decided they cannot yet take it in.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: There is much to say about Melchizedek, and it is hard to explain, since these readers have become dull of hearing (v.11). By now they ought to be teachers, and instead they need the basic principles taught again; they need milk, not solid food (v.12) — and everyone who lives on milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, being a child (v.13). Solid food is for the mature, whose powers of discernment have been trained by constant practice to distinguish good from evil (v.14).
verseByVerse.theology:
What Maturity Actually Is

Verse 14 defines it, and every term does work. “Powers of discernment” is literally the faculties of perception, the word used of the physical senses — moral judgement described as something that perceives directly, the way a tongue tastes. “Trained” is gegymnasmena, the gymnasium word: exercised, put through a regime as an athlete trains a body. And “constant practice” is one word meaning habit, settled usage.

So maturity is not the accumulation of doctrine — these readers may well have known a great deal. It is a trained faculty: the capacity to tell right from wrong quickly and by feel, developed through repetition over a long time. Which is why solid food is withheld. Not because they are unintelligent, but because the organ that would digest it has not been exercised, and no amount of teaching substitutes for use.

There is comfort in that as well as rebuke. If maturity came by intellect, most Christians would be shut out of it. It comes by practice, which is available to everybody — the ordinary believer who has spent thirty years making small decisions in the fear of God has a trained palate, whatever he can or cannot explain.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The decisive word in verse 11 is become. They were not always like this: there was a time when these people were sharp and took the word in eagerly, and stood their ground publicly and lost property for it (10:32–34). The condition was acquired — gradually, and probably without their noticing. That is the drift of 2:1 showing up in the ears. Note too where the writer locates the fault: the subject is “hard to explain” not because it is obscure but since you have become dull of hearing. That is a bold thing for a preacher to say, and he says it without malice, having already called them holy brothers and about to call them beloved.

Now: The rebuke of verse 12 is not that they know little but that they have not moved — “by this time” implies a clock. And the assumption buried in it is quietly demanding: the ordinary trajectory of a believer runs from being taught to being able to explain. Not that everyone should hold office, which James warns against (Jas 3:1), but a person who has been a Christian twenty years and cannot open the gospel to somebody else has, on this letter’s reckoning, stalled. Note also that “unskilled” in verse 13 is literally without experience: the problem with the perpetual beginner is not that he lacks information but that he has never used any.

The diagnostic question this passage puts is worth asking honestly — when a passage of Scripture seems dry, the instinctive conclusion is that the passage is dry. Hebrews raises another possibility, and a person can only test it by asking whether he was always this bored.

verseByVerse.quote: About this we have much to say, and it is hard to explain, since you have become dull of hearing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“About this we have much to say, and it is hard to explain, since you have become dull of hearing.”

The sentence changes the temperature of the letter entirely. The writer has just named Melchizedek twice and is standing at the door of his central argument — and he stops, turns to his congregation, and tells them why he is not going to go on yet.

Read the middle phrase carefully, because the fault is not located where we would expect. It is “hard to explain” — literally hard to interpret — and the reason given is not that the subject is obscure. It is since you have become dull of hearing. The difficulty is in the audience.

That is a bold thing for any preacher to say, and notice that he says it without malice. He has called these people holy brothers (3:1) and will call them beloved (6:9). He is not writing them off; he is telling them the truth about why the sermon is stalling.

“Dull” is nothros, and it means sluggish, slow, torpid — the word could be used of a numb limb or a lazy animal. It is the opposite of the alertness the letter has been urging since 2:1.

And the decisive word is “become”. They were not always like this. There was a time when these people were sharp, when they took the word in eagerly, when they stood their ground publicly and lost property for it — the writer will remind them of exactly that at 10:32–34. They have become dull, which means the condition was acquired, gradually, and probably without their noticing.

That is the drift of 2:1 showing up in the ears. Nobody decides to stop hearing. Attention is not lost in a moment; it seeps away while a person is busy with other things, and the first symptom is that teaching which once thrilled them now seems difficult and rather abstract.

Ask the diagnostic question this verse puts. If a passage of Scripture seems dry, the instinctive conclusion is that the passage is dry. Hebrews raises another possibility — and it is a possibility a person can only test by asking whether he was always this bored.

verseByVerse.quote: For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you again the basic principles of the oracles of God. You need milk, not solid food, for everyone who lives on milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, since he is a child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you again the basic principles.”

The rebuke is not that they know little. It is that they have not moved. “By this time” implies a clock: these were not new converts. Enough years had passed that they should have been instructing others, and instead they need the alphabet again.

Note the assumption buried in it, which is quietly demanding. The normal expectation of a Christian is that he will eventually be able to teach somebody something. Not that everyone should hold office — James warns against a rush to that (Jas 3:1) — but that the ordinary trajectory of a believer runs from being taught to being able to explain. A person who has been a Christian for twenty years and cannot open the gospel to someone else has, on this letter’s reckoning, stalled.

“The basic principles of the oracles of God.” The word for basic principles is stoicheia — the elements, the ABC, the first things in a sequence. Chapter 6 will list them: repentance, faith, washings, laying on of hands, resurrection, judgement.

“You need milk, not solid food.” Paul uses the same image with the Corinthians (1 Cor 3:1–2), and in both places the point is not that milk is bad. Milk is exactly right — for an infant. It becomes a problem only when a person is still on it years later.

Then verse 13 explains what the diet produces: “everyone who lives on milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, since he is a child.”

“Unskilled” is literally without experience — untried, not having handled the thing. The problem with the perpetual beginner is not that he lacks information but that he has never used any. He has heard about righteousness and has no practice in it.

And that reframes the whole rebuke. The writer is not complaining that his readers have not read enough. He is saying that knowledge which is never exercised does not mature anybody — and the next verse will say how maturity actually comes.

verseByVerse.quote: But solid food is for the mature, for those who have their powers of discernment trained by constant practice to distinguish good from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But solid food is for the mature” — and the writer now defines maturity, which is the most practically useful sentence in the chapter.

“For those who have their powers of discernment trained by constant practice to distinguish good from evil.”

Take the terms in order, because every one of them is doing work.

“Powers of discernment” is literally the faculties or organs of perception — the same word used of the physical senses. The writer is describing moral judgement as a sense: something that perceives directly, the way a tongue tastes.

“Trained” is gegymnasmena — the gymnasium word, from which we get gymnastics. It means exercised, put through a training regime, as an athlete trains a body.

“By constant practice” is one word meaning habit, custom, settled usage. Not by intensive study, not by a crisis, not by a conference. By habit.

Put them together and you have a definition of Christian maturity that cuts against the common assumption. Maturity is not the accumulation of doctrine; the writer’s readers may well have known a great deal. It is a trained faculty — the capacity to tell right from wrong quickly and by feel, developed the way an athlete’s reflexes are developed, through repetition over a long time.

And that explains why the writer will not proceed to Melchizedek. Solid food is not withheld from these people because they are unintelligent. It is withheld because the faculty that would digest it has not been exercised, and no amount of teaching substitutes for use.

There is a comfort here as well as a rebuke, and the comfort should not be missed. If maturity came by intellect, most Christians would be excluded from it. It comes by practice, which is available to everybody — the ordinary believer who has spent thirty years making small decisions in the fear of God has a trained palate, whatever he can or cannot explain. And the writer’s next words, at the head of chapter 6, are “let us go on”. He does not leave them there.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>For every high priest chosen from among men is appointed to act on behalf of men in relation to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.<sup>2</sup>He can deal gently with the ignorant and wayward, since he himself is beset with weakness.<sup>3</sup>Because of this he is obligated to offer sacrifice for his own sins just as he does for those of the people.<sup>4</sup>And no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was.<sup>5</sup>So also Christ did not exalt himself to be made a high priest, but was appointed by him who said to him, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you”;<sup>6</sup>as he says also in another place, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”<sup>7</sup>In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence.<sup>8</sup>Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered.<sup>9</sup>And being made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him,<sup>10</sup>being designated by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek.<sup>11</sup>About this we have much to say, and it is hard to explain, since you have become dull of hearing.<sup>12</sup>For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you again the basic principles of the oracles of God. You need milk, not solid food,<sup>13</sup>for everyone who lives on milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, since he is a child.<sup>14</sup>But solid food is for the mature, for those who have their powers of discernment trained by constant practice to distinguish good from evil.

6.title: Press On to Maturity: The Anchor of the Soul
6.overview:
Chapter 6 contains both the most debated and the most encouraging passages in the entire letter. The writer begins with a call to maturity — “let us leave the elementary doctrine of Christ and go on to maturity” — not discarding the foundations but building on them rather than perpetually relaying them. Then he issues the most severe warning in the letter (vv. 4–8): those who have experienced the full light of the gospel and then deliberately fallen away cannot be renewed to repentance. The warning has generated enormous theological debate, but its pastoral purpose is clear: it aims to shock those who are drifting into understanding what is at stake.

Immediately after the warning, however, the writer pivots with extraordinary pastoral grace: “though we speak in this way, yet in your case, beloved, we feel sure of better things” (v. 9). The warning is real but it is not his assessment of his readers’ condition; it is the description of where the trajectory of drift leads. He is confident they will not go there. And to ground that confidence, he points not to their performance but to God’s faithfulness: God is not unjust; he will not forget their work and love.

The chapter closes with one of the most beautiful images in Scripture: hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure, reaching through the veil into the inner sanctuary where Jesus has gone as a forerunner. The same veil that once sealed off the Most Holy Place from all but the high priest is now the anchor-point of the believer’s hope. Everything is secure because the Priest is already there, already inside, already interceding.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Hardest Warning, and the Confidence After It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Let us leave the elementary doctrine and go on to maturity, not laying the foundation again — repentance and faith (v.1), washings, laying on of hands, resurrection, eternal judgement (v.2) — and this we will do if God permits (v.3). For it is impossible, in the case of those once enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift and shared in the Holy Spirit (v.4), and tasted the goodness of God’s word and the powers of the age to come (v.5), and then have fallen away, to restore them again to repentance, since they are crucifying the Son of God again and holding him up to contempt (v.6).

Land that drinks the rain and bears a useful crop receives blessing (v.7); land that bears thorns and thistles is worthless and near to being cursed, and its end is burning (v.8). Yet in your case, beloved, we feel sure of better things — things that belong to salvation (v.9); for God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love you have shown in serving the saints, as you still do (v.10). And we desire each one of you to show the same earnestness for full assurance of hope to the end (v.11), so that you may not be sluggish but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises (v.12).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Passage Set Out Honestly

This is the most disputed sentence in the letter, and sincere Christians read it differently; a reader in distress deserves to see the ground. Some hold it describes true believers who genuinely lose salvation — but the letter says Christ saves to the uttermost and always lives to intercede (7:25), and on that reading the loss would be irreversible, which few who take the line actually teach. Some hold it is hypothetical: if such a thing happened restoration would be impossible, but it does not happen — which fits the theology and reads thinly against the urgency. The reading that best fits the letter’s own vocabulary is that these came very close and were never united to Christ (cf. 1 John 2:19).

The decisive observation is what the list of privileges does not contain. Enlightened, tasted, shared, tasted — every term describes something received, experienced or seen. Not one says justified, born again, forgiven, or loved by God. Compare verse 9, where the writer calls the same congregation beloved and speaks of things that belong to salvation. He can use that language when he wants to, and in verses 4–5 he does not.

And whichever reading one holds, the pastoral force is identical — which is presumably why it was left as it is. The warning is not addressed to the anxious. A person terrified that this describes him is displaying exactly the softness of heart the passage says is absent; you cannot repent of having become unable to repent. The people in view are not agonising. They have walked out.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Notice what is in the foundation of verses 1–2: repentance, faith in God, ceremonial washings, laying on of hands, resurrection, judgement. There is nothing distinctively Christian in the list — a devout Pharisee would have affirmed the lot. Which sharpens the complaint considerably: these readers were stalled precisely where Judaism and Christianity overlap, and had never built anything above the shared foundation. That is exactly why going back looked so easy. And “leave” the foundation does not mean abandon it — you abandon a foundation by digging it up every few years to check it is still there, which is what they were doing.

Now: The parable of the field settles what the privileges prove. Two plots under the same sky, drinking the same rain, cultivated the same way — and one produces a harvest and the other a thornbush. What distinguishes them is not the rain but the soil, and the only way to tell them apart is to wait and see what grows. Note the writer’s carefulness: the bad field is not cursed but near to being cursed, and near is not yet. Then he applies the test himself in verse 10 — the evidence for his confidence is the crop: work, love, and service to the saints, as you still do. They are dull of hearing and stalled in understanding, and they are still looking after people, and he treats that as decisive.

There is comfort in the double negative for anyone whose service has gone unnoticed: God is not unjust so as to overlook it. He may be the only one who has not.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us leave the elementary doctrine of Christ and go on to maturity, not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God, and of instruction about washings, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. And this we will do if God permits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Therefore let us leave the elementary doctrine of Christ and go on to maturity.”

“Leave” sounds alarming until the metaphor is seen. The image is a building, and the next clause makes it explicit: “not laying again a foundation”. You do not abandon a foundation by building on it. You abandon it by digging it up every few years to check it is still there.

That is what these readers were doing. Not denying the basics — endlessly returning to them, and never getting a wall up.

“Let us” is worth noticing too. The preacher includes himself, as he does in every warning. He is not standing on the finished storey calling down.

Then six items in three pairs, and they are the foundation he means.

Repentance from dead works and faith toward God — the two sides of conversion, turning from and turning to. Instruction about washings and the laying on of hands — almost certainly the rites of initiation, and the plural “washings” is the ordinary word for ceremonial cleansings rather than the usual term for baptism, which suggests teaching Jewish converts how Christian baptism differed from the washings they knew. The resurrection of the dead and eternal judgement — what happens at the end.

And here is the striking thing about the list: there is nothing distinctively Christian in it. Every item could have been taught in a synagogue. Repentance, faith in God, ceremonial washing, laying on of hands, resurrection, judgement — a devout Pharisee would have affirmed the lot.

Which sharpens the writer’s complaint considerably. His readers were stalled precisely at the point where Judaism and Christianity overlap. They had never moved on to what is peculiar to Christ — his priesthood, his sacrifice, his finished work — and that is exactly why going back looked so easy. If you have not yet built anything above the shared foundation, stepping off it costs you nothing you can see.

“And this we will do if God permits.” A small qualifier with considerable weight. Progress in understanding is not simply a matter of resolve; it is granted. The writer intends to press on, and knows that whether his readers actually advance is not finally in his gift.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is impossible, in the case of those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, and have shared in the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the age to come,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For it is impossible…” — and the sentence that begins here is the most disputed in the letter and among the most disputed in Scripture. Go slowly, and worth saying at the outset that sincere Christians have read it differently.

Notice first that the word “impossible” stands at the head of the Greek sentence, in the emphatic position, and that its object does not arrive until verse 6: impossible to restore them again to repentance. Everything between is description of the people in view.

Five things are said about them, and they are not small.

“Once been enlightened” — and “once” here is the word for once-for-all. Light has fallen on them; they have seen.

“Have tasted the heavenly gift.” Some have tried to soften “tasted” into a sip rather than a meal, but the letter itself forbids it: at 2:9 Jesus tasted death for everyone, and he did not sample it. The word means real experience.

“Have shared in the Holy Spirit.” The word is the one used at 3:1 of sharing a heavenly calling and at 3:14 of sharing in Christ.

“Have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the age to come.” They have found Scripture good, and they have seen the future break into the present — miracles, the gifts the writer mentioned at 2:4.

Any honest reader has to concede that this is a formidable description. It is not a list of things that could be said of a person who had merely attended. Whatever the passage finally means, it cannot be dismissed by saying these people were obviously never involved at all.

And yet the writer has chosen his words with care, and one thing is conspicuously absent from the list. Every term describes something received, experienced, or seen. Not one of them says these people were justified, born again, forgiven, or loved by God. Compare what he says of the same congregation nine verses later: beloved, and things that belong to salvation. He can use that language when he wants to, and here he does not.

verseByVerse.quote: and then have fallen away, to restore them again to repentance, since they are crucifying once again the Son of God to their own harm and holding him up to contempt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And then have fallen away, to restore them again to repentance.”

The word for falling away is a strong one — it means to fall alongside, to defect. It is not stumbling into sin. It is the deliberate abandonment the letter has been warning about since 3:12, standing off from the living God.

And the reason is given: “since they are crucifying once again the Son of God to their own harm and holding him up to contempt.” Both participles are present and continuous — while they are doing this. A person in the act of publicly repudiating Christ cannot simultaneously be repenting of it.

“Holding him up to contempt” is a public word, used of exposing someone to open shame. This is not a private lapse. These are people who have gone back and said, before witnesses, that the crucified man was rightly crucified.

Now the interpretations, set out plainly, because a reader in distress deserves to see the ground.

Some hold the passage describes true believers who genuinely lose salvation. The difficulty is that the letter itself says Christ saves to the uttermost and always lives to intercede (7:25), and by that reading the loss would be irreversible — which few who take this line actually teach.

Some hold it is hypothetical: if such a thing happened, restoration would be impossible — but it does not happen. That fits the theology and reads a little thinly against the urgency of the warning.

The reading that best fits the letter’s own vocabulary is that these are people who came very close and were never united to Christ — who saw the light, tasted the gift, shared in the Spirit’s work among them, watched the miracles, and finally turned and repudiated it. That is what the field in the next two verses will illustrate, and what John describes when he says they went out from us because they were not of us (1 John 2:19).

And whichever reading one holds, the pastoral force is identical, which is presumably why the writer left it as he did. The warning is not addressed to the anxious. A person terrified that this describes him is displaying precisely the softness of heart the passage says is absent — you cannot repent of having become unable to repent. The people in view are not agonising. They have walked out.

verseByVerse.quote: For land that has drunk the rain that often falls on it, and produces a crop useful to those for whose sake it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God. But if it bears thorns and thistles, it is worthless and near to being cursed, and its end is to be burned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer illustrates, and the picture explains more than the argument does.

“Land that has drunk the rain that often falls on it.” One field. The rain is the same, the frequency is the same, the cultivation is the same. And the ground has genuinely absorbed it — drunk is the word, which corresponds exactly to the tasting and sharing of verses 4 and 5.

Then two outcomes from identical treatment. One plot “produces a crop useful to those for whose sake it is cultivated” and “receives a blessing from God”. The other “bears thorns and thistles” and is “worthless and near to being cursed, and its end is to be burned”.

The image settles what the privileges of verses 4–5 actually prove, and that is the reason it is here. Rain falling on ground and being absorbed does not determine what comes up. Two fields under the same sky, drinking the same water, produce a harvest and a thornbush. What distinguishes them is not the rain but the nature of the soil — and the only way to tell them apart is to wait and see what grows.

“Thorns and thistles” is not a random pair. It is the exact phrase of the curse in Eden (Gen 3:18). The unfruitful ground is doing what cursed ground does.

Note also the writer’s carefulness, which is easily missed and matters enormously. He does not say the second field is cursed. He says it is “near to being cursed”. Near is not yet. As long as a field is only near, there is time for something else to come up — and the whole letter is written to make that happen.

The parable also answers the pastoral question the previous verses raise. If both fields look identical while the rain is falling, how does anyone know? The answer is: by the crop. Not by the intensity of the experience, not by how much was tasted, but by what is growing now — which is precisely what the writer turns to in the very next verse.

verseByVerse.quote: Though we speak in this way, yet in your case, beloved, we feel sure of better things—things that belong to salvation. For God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name in serving the saints, as you still do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Though we speak in this way, yet in your case, beloved…”

It is the only time in the letter he uses that word, and he uses it here — immediately after the severest paragraph he has written. Whatever the warning was for, it was not to tell these people he had given up on them.

“We feel sure of better things — things that belong to salvation.” The verb means to be persuaded, convinced. He is not being polite. He has just described people who fall away, and he says: that is not you, and I am confident of it.

Note the language he now permits himself. “Things that belong to salvation” — the very category conspicuously absent from the list in verses 4–5. He knows the difference and writes accordingly.

Then the ground of his confidence, and it is not what we might expect: “For God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name in serving the saints, as you still do.”

The evidence is the crop. The parable asked how you tell one field from another, and the writer now points at what is growing in this one: work, love, and service to other Christians — continuing, since he adds “as you still do”. They may be dull of hearing and stalled in understanding, and they are still looking after people. That is fruit, and he treats it as decisive.

The phrasing repays care, because it could be misread as saying God owes them. It says the opposite of that and something better. God is not unjust — he does not forget. It is not that their service has earned salvation; it is that a God who had produced such fruit and then discarded the field would be acting unjustly toward his own work.

And there is real pastoral comfort in the double negative for anyone whose service has gone unnoticed. The meals taken to a sick house, the years of unremarkable faithfulness to awkward people — God is not unjust so as to overlook it. He may be the only one who has not.

verseByVerse.quote: And we desire each one of you to show the same earnestness to have the full assurance of hope until the end, so that you may not be sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And we desire each one of you” — the individual concern again, as at 3:12 and 4:1. He has just expressed confidence about the congregation as a body; he will not let that confidence become a blanket that covers someone quietly slipping.

“To show the same earnestness” — the same as they have shown in serving the saints. He is not asking them to start something new. He is asking them to apply to their hope the diligence they already apply to their neighbours.

“To have the full assurance of hope until the end.” The word for full assurance means being carried to the full, brought to complete conviction. And notice that assurance is here something to be pursued. It is not merely a feeling that arrives or fails to; it is a state a Christian may work toward, and the writer thinks earnestness is how.

“So that you may not be sluggish.” The word is nothros — the same one used at 5:11, where they had become dull of hearing. He is joining the two: sluggish ears and sluggish lives are the same condition, and the remedy for both is the same earnestness.

“But imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.” And here the letter turns a corner that will not be completed until chapter 11. Against the dullness, examples — real people who waited and received.

“Faith and patience” is the pairing that runs to the end of the letter. Makrothymia is long-temperedness, the endurance that keeps going when the promise is slow. Faith takes God at his word; patience keeps taking him at it for years.

That is what these readers were short of. Not information — they had the foundation. Not zeal at the start — they had stood their ground and lost property for it. What had run out was the long, unglamorous willingness to keep believing a promise that had not yet arrived, and the writer knows exactly which patriarch to produce as the answer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — Two Unchangeable Things, and an Anchor Behind the Curtain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God promised Abraham, having no one greater to swear by, he swore by himself (v.13): surely I will bless you and multiply you (v.14). And thus Abraham, having patiently waited, obtained the promise (v.15). People swear by something greater than themselves, and an oath ends all dispute (v.16); so God, desiring to show the heirs of the promise the unchangeable character of his purpose, guaranteed it with an oath (v.17), so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast the hope set before us (v.18). We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, entering the inner place behind the curtain (v.19), where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf, having become a high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek (v.20).
verseByVerse.theology:
An Anchor That Goes Upward

The anchor was a common emblem of security, and the two adjectives are precise — sure, it will not fail in itself; steadfast, it will not shift under strain. A bad anchor fails either by breaking or by dragging. But the writer immediately does what nobody else does with the image: an anchor goes down, and this one goes up and in, entering the place behind the curtain — the veil of the Most Holy Place, which no one crossed but the high priest, once a year, with blood.

So the cable runs out of this world altogether and is made fast inside the sanctuary. The storm and the anchorage are in different places: a ship in heavy weather is held by ground it cannot see, and the state of the sea has no bearing on the holding. For a congregation whose property had been seized and whose neighbours had turned, that is the whole point.

Then prodromos, forerunner — used of scouts sent ahead of an army, and of the small boat that carried an anchor forward into harbour when a ship could not get in against the wind: rowed ahead, the anchor dropped inside, and the ship then hauled in to where the anchor already was. A forerunner is not merely someone who has arrived; he goes first so that others follow. The high priest of old went behind the curtain alone and came out again, and nobody followed him. This one went in and stayed, and the rope is attached to us.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The oath to Abraham was sworn on the mountain of Genesis 22, immediately after the knife was raised over Isaac — the point at which the promise looked most impossible and the man had proved he would trust God with it anyway. The logic of an oath is to invoke something greater as surety, and God has no such thing available, so he swore by himself: for the promise to fail he would have to cease to be God. And note the astonishing reason given in verse 17 — he did it because he desired to show more convincingly. His bare word is already as reliable as anything in the universe and an oath cannot make him more truthful. It adds nothing to God and everything to our confidence, and he swore it for that reason alone.

Now: Put the years against verse 15. Abraham was seventy-five when the promise came and a hundred when Isaac was born — twenty-five years, most of them with no evidence whatever, through a stretch in which he twice tried to arrange the outcome himself and once laughed at God for suggesting it. The waiting was not serene; it was long and patchy, and Hebrews still calls it patience. What the New Testament commends in Abraham is not that he never wobbled but that he was still there at the end.

Note too that the letter’s two impossibilities now face each other: it is impossible to restore an apostate (v.4), and it is impossible for God to lie (v.18). The second is the one to build on. And “fled for refuge” is drawn from the cities of refuge (Num 35), where a man ran for his life pursued by the avenger of blood — safe inside, dead outside, and the running undignified and absolutely necessary. It is not a flattering picture of a Christian, and it is an accurate one.

verseByVerse.quote: For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself, saying, “Surely I will bless you and multiply you.” And thus Abraham, having patiently waited, obtained the promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For when God made a promise to Abraham…” Here is the example, and he is the obvious one. To Jewish readers Abraham was the father of the nation and the pattern of faith — and the writer is about to make him the pattern of waiting.

“Since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself.” The occasion is Genesis 22, on the mountain, immediately after Abraham had raised the knife over Isaac — the point at which the promise looked most impossible and the man had proved he would trust God with it anyway.

The logic of an oath is that you invoke something greater than yourself as surety. God has no such thing available. So he swore by himself, which means the guarantee of the promise is his own existence: for it to fail he would have to cease to be God.

“Surely I will bless you and multiply you.” The quotation is compressed — Genesis says more — and the writer takes the two verbs that matter for his purpose.

Then verse 15, and everything hangs on the middle phrase: “And thus Abraham, having patiently waited, obtained the promise.”

Put the years against it. Abraham was seventy-five when the promise was first made and a hundred when Isaac was born. Twenty-five years, most of them with no evidence whatever, and through a stretch in which he twice tried to arrange the outcome himself and once laughed at God for suggesting it. The waiting was not serene. It was long and it was patchy, and Hebrews still calls it patience.

That should be a comfort to anybody measuring their own faith against the patriarchs. What the New Testament commends in Abraham is not that he never wobbled; it is that he was still there at the end.

And “obtained the promise” needs a note, because the writer will say something apparently opposite at 11:13 — these all died not having received the things promised. He received Isaac; he did not receive the city or the nation or the blessing to all peoples. The promise was kept and it was not yet finished, which is exactly the position of the letter’s readers.

verseByVerse.quote: For people swear by something greater than themselves, and in all their disputes an oath is final for confirmation. So when God desired to show more convincingly to the heirs of the promise the unchangeable character of his purpose, he guaranteed it with an oath, so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“People swear by something greater than themselves, and in all their disputes an oath is final for confirmation.”

The writer explains why oaths exist at all. Human beings are not reliably truthful, so societies devise a mechanism for ending argument: you call something greater to witness, and the matter is closed. An oath is the point at which a dispute stops.

“So when God desired to show more convincingly… he guaranteed it with an oath.”

Sit with that for a moment, because it is astonishing. God’s bare word is already as reliable as anything in the universe; an oath cannot make him more truthful. He did it because he wanted to convince us. The oath adds nothing to God and everything to our confidence, and he swore it for that reason alone.

“To the heirs of the promise.” And notice that the oath sworn on a mountain to one old man is described as made for the benefit of everyone who would ever inherit it. That includes the congregation hearing this letter, and it includes anyone reading it now.

“By two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie.” The two are the promise and the oath — his word, and his word sworn. And “impossible” is the same word that opened verse 4. The letter’s two impossibilities face each other: it is impossible to restore an apostate, and it is impossible for God to lie. The second is the one to build on.

“We who have fled for refuge.” The phrase is drawn from the cities of refuge (Num 35), where a man who had killed accidentally ran for his life to a walled town, pursued by the avenger of blood. He was safe inside and dead outside, and the running was undignified and absolutely necessary.

That is the writer’s picture of a Christian, and it is not a flattering one. Not a seeker weighing options but a man running for his life to the only place that will hold him.

“Might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us.” And there is the purpose of the whole paragraph. God swore an oath so that frightened people would keep their grip.

verseByVerse.quote: We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters into the inner place behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf, having become a high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul.”

The image was common enough — anchors appear on ancient tombs and coins as emblems of security — and the two adjectives are precise: sure, meaning it will not fail in itself, and steadfast, meaning it will not shift under strain. A bad anchor fails either by breaking or by dragging.

But the writer immediately does something no one else does with the metaphor, and it is the making of the passage. An anchor goes down. This one goes up and in: “a hope that enters into the inner place behind the curtain.”

The curtain is the veil of the Most Holy Place — the barrier no one crossed but the high priest, once a year, with blood. That is where the anchor is lodged. Not in circumstances, not in the believer’s own steadiness, not even in the visible church. The cable runs out of this world altogether and is made fast inside the sanctuary of God.

Which means the storm and the anchorage are in different places. A ship in heavy weather is held by ground it cannot see, and the state of the sea has no bearing on the holding. For a congregation whose property had been seized and whose neighbours had turned, that is the entire point.

“Where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf.” And the metaphor changes again, into something more startling still.

“Forerunner” is prodromos. It was used of scouts sent ahead of an army, and of the small boat that carried an anchor forward into harbour when a ship could not get in against the wind — rowed ahead, dropped the anchor inside, and the ship was then hauled in to where the anchor already was.

That is the word, and it makes the picture complete. A forerunner is not merely someone who has arrived; he is someone who goes first so that others follow. The high priest of old went behind the curtain alone and came out again, and nobody followed him. This one went in and stayed, and the rope is attached to us.

“Having become a high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.” The name returns for the third time, and now the writer has his congregation where he wants them: warned, reassured, anchored, and ready. Chapter 7 begins the argument he broke off at 5:11.
