7.title: The Order of Melchizedek: A Priest Forever
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is the theological center of Hebrews and one of the most original pieces of biblical theology in the New Testament. From two spare Old Testament references — the brief narrative of Genesis 14:17–20 (Abraham’s encounter with Melchizedek after the battle of the kings) and the single line of Psalm 110:4 (“You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek”) — the writer constructs a sustained argument for the absolute supremacy and finality of Jesus’ priesthood over the entire Levitical system.

The argument from Melchizedek’s typological significance is breathtaking in its detail. He was king of righteousness, king of peace, priest of God Most High — three offices in one person. He appeared without recorded genealogy, without recorded birth or death — and this literary silence, the writer argues, is itself theologically significant: it makes Melchizedek a type of the eternal Son of God, who truly has no beginning or end. Abraham, the father of the entire covenant people, gave him a tenth of everything and received his blessing — which means Melchizedek was greater than Abraham and, since Levi was seminally present in Abraham, greater than the entire Levitical priesthood.

The implications are categorical: if the Levitical priesthood had brought perfection, why would God promise another priest after a different order? The fact of Psalm 110:4 is the proof that the Levitical system was always provisional, always pointing forward, always inadequate as a final word. Jesus is the final word: a priest not on the basis of legal descent but on the basis of “the power of an indestructible life” (v. 16). His priesthood never ends. His intercession never fails. He is “able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him” (v. 25) — completely, finally, without remainder or qualification.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Melchizedek, and What Abraham Did
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the Most High God, met Abraham returning from battle and blessed him (v.1), and Abraham gave him a tenth of everything — his name meaning king of righteousness, and Salem meaning peace (v.2). Without father, mother or genealogy, with neither beginning of days nor end of life, resembling the Son of God, he continues a priest forever (v.3).

See how great he was, that the patriarch gave him a tenth of the spoils (v.4). The Levites take tithes by commandment, from their own brothers (v.5); but this man, not descended from them, received tithes from Abraham and blessed the holder of the promises (v.6) — and it is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior (v.7). In one case mortal men receive tithes, in the other one of whom it is testified that he lives (v.8). One might even say Levi paid tithes through Abraham (v.9), being still in his ancestor’s loins when Melchizedek met him (v.10).
verseByVerse.theology:
Reading the Silence of Scripture

Verse 3 has been taken to mean Melchizedek was an angel or the pre-incarnate Christ. Both readings founder on the last clause, which says he resembles the Son of God — and a thing does not resemble itself. What the writer is doing is reading a deliberate silence. Genesis is a book of genealogies, telling you who fathered whom and how long they lived, for chapter after chapter; Melchizedek walks in with none of it.

For a priest that absence is extraordinary, because the Levitical priesthood was entirely a matter of documentation — after the exile, men who could not produce the records were excluded as unclean (Ezra 2:61–62). Melchizedek has no papers whatever, and Scripture calls him a priest of the Most High God. So Genesis has drawn a portrait with the genealogy left out, sketching a priesthood that does not depend on descent and does not end at a funeral. Note the direction of the comparison too: the writer does not say Christ is like Melchizedek but that Melchizedek was made to resemble the Son. The eternal reality came first; the man in Genesis is the sketch.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The whole case rests on two customs the readers understood perfectly — who pays tithes to whom, and who blesses whom. Blessing runs downhill: father to son, priest to people, king to subject, and nobody blesses upward. So Abraham, carrying the promise and the father of the nation, put himself in the lower position twice in one afternoon. These readers had been reading Genesis 14 all their lives and had never noticed what it implied. Note also the order of the names in verse 2 — righteousness first, then peace — which is the shape of the gospel and cannot be reversed. There is no peace with God that does not come by way of righteousness, which is why a merely merciful God who waived the problem would have given us neither.

Now: Verses 9–10 press the point through representative solidarity, and the writer knows it: “one might even say”. Levi was born a century later and, in the Hebrew way of reckoning, was genuinely present in his ancestor. That is not a curiosity but the logic of the whole Bible — it is why the sin of one man could involve a race and why the obedience of one man can save one (Rom 5:12–19). A reader who finds representative solidarity strange will find most of the doctrine of salvation strange, since it all runs on the same principle.

verseByVerse.quote: For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, and to him Abraham apportioned a tenth part of everything. He is first, by translation of his name, king of righteousness, and then he is also king of Salem, that is, king of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The argument broken off at 5:11 resumes, and everything now turns on a man who appears in three verses of Genesis and is never mentioned again in the Old Testament except in one line of one psalm.

The episode is Genesis 14. Abraham has just rescued his nephew Lot by defeating a coalition of kings, and on the way home a stranger comes out to meet him: Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God. He brings bread and wine, blesses Abraham, receives a tenth of the spoil, and vanishes from the narrative.

“Priest of the Most High God” is the arresting phrase. This is centuries before Sinai, before Levi is born, before there is any Israelite priesthood at all — and here is a Canaanite king who is already a priest of the true God, and Abraham recognises him as such.

Then the writer works on the names, and the method needs understanding rather than dismissed. He is not inventing meanings; he is reading the text the way its own authors read names, as carrying significance.

Melchizedek divides into melek, king, and tsedeq, righteousness — king of righteousness. And Salem is shalem, cognate with shalom — king of peace. Salem is almost certainly the old name for Jerusalem (Ps 76:2), which adds a further resonance the writer does not press.

And note the order, which he does press: “first… and then”. Righteousness first, then peace. That is not decoration but the shape of the gospel, and the order cannot be reversed. There is no peace with God that does not come by way of righteousness — which is why the cross was necessary and why a merely merciful God who waived the problem would have given us neither.

“To him Abraham apportioned a tenth part of everything.” That detail will carry the whole argument of verses 4–10. Abraham, the father of the nation, the man to whom the promises were made, handed over a tithe — and a tithe is what you give to a superior.

verseByVerse.quote: He is without father or mother or genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but resembling the Son of God he continues a priest forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“He is without father or mother or genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life.”

This verse has been read as meaning Melchizedek was a supernatural being — an angel, or an appearance of the pre-incarnate Christ. Both readings run into the last clause of the verse, which says he resembles the Son of God. A thing does not resemble itself.

What the writer is doing is reading the silence of Scripture, and it is a recognised way of arguing that his readers would have followed easily. Genesis is a book of genealogies — it tells you who fathered whom, how long they lived, and when they died, for chapter after chapter. Melchizedek walks into the narrative with none of it. No father, no mother, no ancestry, no birth, no death.

For a priest that absence is extraordinary, because the Levitical priesthood was entirely a matter of documentation. A man’s right to serve depended on proving his descent, and after the exile men who could not produce the records were excluded from the priesthood as unclean (Ezra 2:61–62). Melchizedek has no papers whatever, and Scripture presents him as a priest of the Most High God.

So the silence is not an accident of an incomplete record. The writer takes it as deliberate: Genesis has drawn a portrait with the genealogy left out, in order to sketch a priesthood that does not depend on descent and does not end with a funeral.

“But resembling the Son of God he continues a priest forever.” And note the direction of the comparison, because it is easy to get backwards. The writer does not say Christ is like Melchizedek. He says Melchizedek was made to resemble the Son of God. The eternal reality came first; the man in Genesis is the sketch.

“Continues a priest forever” is true of Melchizedek only in the sense that the text never records him stopping. It is true of Christ absolutely, and that is the point of the whole chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: See how great this man was to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils! And those descendants of Levi who receive the priestly office have a commandment in the law to take tithes from the people, that is, from their brothers, though these also are descended from Abraham. But this man who does not have his descent from them received tithes from Abraham and blessed him who had the promises. It is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“See how great this man was” — and the writer now builds his case on two customs his readers understood perfectly: who pays tithes to whom, and who blesses whom.

“To whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils.” The title is deliberate. Not simply Abraham but the patriarch — the founder, the greatest name a Jewish reader possessed. Whatever is proved about Melchizedek is proved against the highest possible standard.

Then the comparison in verse 5. The sons of Levi “have a commandment in the law to take tithes from the people” — and note the qualification the writer adds: “that is, from their brothers, though these also are descended from Abraham.” The Levites collected from their own relatives, on the authority of a written command, from people of exactly the same standing as themselves.

Melchizedek did neither. He “does not have his descent from them”, he had no legal warrant to collect, and the man who paid him was not a brother but Abraham himself. The tithe was given, not levied.

“And blessed him who had the promises.” This is the second and stronger argument. Abraham was the man who held the promises of God — and he stood there and received a blessing from a stranger.

“It is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior.” The writer states it as a self-evident social fact, and in that world it was. Blessing runs downhill: father to son, priest to people, king to subject. Nobody blesses upward.

So Abraham — who was carrying the promise, the father of the nation, the man in whom all families of the earth would be blessed — put himself in the lower position twice in a single afternoon, and Genesis records it without comment. The writer’s readers had been reading that chapter all their lives and had never noticed what it implied.

verseByVerse.quote: In the one case tithes are received by mortal men, but in the other case, by one of whom it is testified that he lives. One might even say that Levi himself, who receives tithes, paid tithes through Abraham, for he was still in the loins of his ancestor when Melchizedek met him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“In the one case tithes are received by mortal men, but in the other case, by one of whom it is testified that he lives.”

The contrast is between men who die and a man whose death is not recorded. And the writer is careful with his language: not “who lives” but “of whom it is testified that he lives” — the claim rests on what the text says and does not say, which is exactly the argument of verse 3.

The Levitical priesthood was a relay. Aaron served and died; Eleazar took the robes; and so on for fourteen centuries, every generation burying its high priest and consecrating another. The system was designed around mortality.

Then verses 9–10, and the writer knows he is pressing hard: “One might even say that Levi himself, who receives tithes, paid tithes through Abraham, for he was still in the loins of his ancestor when Melchizedek met him.”

The qualifier is a nice touch. He is not claiming this as a knock-down proof; he is offering it as a way of seeing the thing. Levi was Abraham’s great-grandson and was not born for another century — and in the Hebrew way of reckoning, a descendant is genuinely present in his ancestor and acts in him.

That way of thinking is not a curiosity. It is the logic of the whole Bible. It is why the sin of one man could involve a race (Rom 5:12–19), and why the obedience of one man can save one. A modern reader who finds representative solidarity strange will find most of the doctrine of salvation strange, since it all runs on the same principle.

So the conclusion stands: the tribe that would one day collect Israel’s tithes had already, in its ancestor, paid them to somebody else. The Levitical priesthood acknowledged a greater priesthood before it existed — and Genesis 14 has been sitting in the Torah all along saying so.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–28 — A Priest Forever, and the Change That Follows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If perfection had come through the Levitical priesthood, why announce another after the order of Melchizedek (v.11)? For a change of priesthood requires a change of law (v.12) — and the one spoken of belonged to a tribe from which none ever served at the altar (v.13), since our Lord descended from Judah, about which Moses said nothing concerning priests (v.14). Another priest arises in Melchizedek’s likeness (v.15), made a priest not by a legal requirement about bodily descent but by the power of an indestructible life (v.16), as it is witnessed: you are a priest forever (v.17).

So a former commandment is set aside for its weakness and uselessness (v.18) — for the law made nothing perfect — and a better hope is introduced, through which we draw near to God (v.19). And it was not without an oath: the former priests were made such without one (v.20), but this one with an oath from him who said, the Lord has sworn and will not change his mind (v.21). This makes Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant (v.22).

The former priests were many, because death prevented them continuing (v.23); he holds his priesthood permanently, continuing forever (v.24). Consequently he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to intercede (v.25). Such a high priest was fitting — holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners, exalted above the heavens (v.26) — with no need to offer daily sacrifices first for himself, since he did this once for all when he offered up himself (v.27). The law appoints weak men; the word of the oath, later than the law, appoints a Son made perfect forever (v.28).
verseByVerse.theology:
Change the Priesthood and the Law Must Follow

Verse 12 is the moment the letter’s argument becomes irreversible. These readers were being drawn back to temple, sacrifices, food laws and calendar, and told — quite correctly — that these were God’s own commands. The writer agrees they were. And he says the entire structure was attached to a priesthood, that God himself has changed the priesthood, and that a superstructure does not outlive its foundation. Not that the law was bad or was disobeyed, but that its basis has been replaced by the God who laid it.

The two qualifications in verse 16 put the difference at its sharpest. One priesthood rests on “a legal requirement concerning bodily descent” — a rule about pedigree, so that a godly Israelite from the wrong tribe could not serve and an indifferent one from the right family could. The other rests on “the power of an indestructible life”, a word meaning undissolvable: not a life that happens to continue but one that cannot be ended. The first is guaranteed by records that can be lost. The second by an empty tomb.

And “weakness and uselessness” (v.18) must be read exactly. These are judgements about capacity for a particular purpose, not verdicts on the law’s worth. It was perfectly effective at exposing sin, regulating a nation and pointing forward; it was useless for making anything perfect, which it never claimed to do. A thermometer is useless for heating a room, and the fault is not in the thermometer.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verse 20 rests on an observation anyone can verify: the whole Levitical arrangement was instituted by command — Exodus and Leviticus are full of instructions about the priesthood — and God never once swears to it. An arrangement made by command can be amended by a later command, and in fact was. An arrangement established by the oath of a God who finds lying impossible (6:18) cannot be. And engyos in verse 22 occurs nowhere else in the New Testament: a surety, the man who stands behind an obligation with his own property and person. Covenants fail because one party does, which is what happened to the first one — and Jesus is not the covenant’s administrator or witness but its guarantor, standing behind it with himself.

Now: Verse 25 is where the chapter cashes out. “To the uttermost” can mean completely or forever, and both are true: he saves entirely, leaving nothing unfinished, and permanently, without expiry. The only qualification named is “those who draw near” — not those who understand, or who have never failed, but those who come. And the ground is what he is doing now: he always lives to intercede. At three in the morning, when a Christian is too tired or ashamed to pray for himself, somebody at the right hand of God is praying for him and has not paused. Note finally the last three words of verse 27. Every other priest offered something else — a bull, a goat, a lamb. This one had nothing to bring but himself, and brought it: priest and sacrifice in one person, which no religious system had ever imagined.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if perfection had been attainable through the Levitical priesthood (for under it the people received the law), what further need would there have been for another priest to arise after the order of Melchizedek, rather than one named after the order of Aaron? For when there is a change in the priesthood, there is necessarily a change in the law as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the argument turns from Genesis to the psalm, and the question is put with real force.

“If perfection had been attainable through the Levitical priesthood… what further need would there have been for another priest?”

The logic is simple and unanswerable. Psalm 110 was written by David, centuries into the Levitical system, and in it God announces a priest of a different order. You do not announce a replacement for something that is working. The very existence of the promise is evidence that the arrangement it replaces was not final.

“Perfection” here means completion, the bringing of a thing to its intended end — the same root as the “made perfect” of 2:10 and 5:9. The question is not whether the Levitical priesthood was good but whether it could finish anything.

And the parenthesis matters: “(for under it the people received the law)”. Priesthood and law are not two separate systems that happen to coexist. The law was given through a priestly arrangement and depends on it; you cannot keep one and discard the other.

Which is exactly what verse 12 says, and it is one of the most consequential sentences in the letter: “For when there is a change in the priesthood, there is necessarily a change in the law as well.”

Follow what that means for the people receiving this letter. They were being drawn back to the temple, the sacrifices, the food laws, the calendar — and being told, no doubt, that these were God’s own commands and could not simply be dropped. The writer agrees that they were God’s commands. And he says the entire structure was attached to a priesthood, and that God himself has changed the priesthood, and that the law therefore cannot stand as it did.

This is the moment the letter’s argument becomes irreversible. Not that the law was bad, not that it was disobeyed, but that its foundation has been replaced by the God who laid it — and a superstructure does not outlive its foundation.

verseByVerse.quote: For the one of whom these things are spoken belonged to another tribe, from which no one has ever served at the altar. For it is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah, and in connection with that tribe Moses said nothing about priests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The one of whom these things are spoken belonged to another tribe, from which no one has ever served at the altar.”

The writer now names the constitutional obstacle. Under the law, priesthood was a matter of tribe, and the boundary was absolute. Not a single man from Judah had ever served at the altar in fourteen hundred years.

“For it is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah.” Note the word. It is common knowledge, not a claim requiring proof — the genealogies were public, and the messianic expectation had always been that the deliverer would come from Judah and from David.

So the two requirements collided. The Messiah had to be from Judah, because the promise said so. A priest had to be from Levi, because the law said so. And Psalm 110 says the Messiah will be a priest.

“In connection with that tribe Moses said nothing about priests.” Once again the argument runs on a silence, as it did with Melchizedek’s genealogy. The law is not merely quiet about priests from Judah; its quietness is the point. There was no provision, because the priesthood being announced was never going to run through the law at all.

This is the answer to an objection the readers would certainly have heard. Anyone defending the old arrangement could say, quite correctly, that Jesus had no right to priestly office — he was not a Levite, he had never served, and the law was explicit.

The writer concedes every word of it. Jesus has no claim to the Levitical priesthood whatever, and never claimed one. He holds a different office, older than Levi and established by an oath the law knew nothing about — which is precisely why the objection, though true, misses everything.

verseByVerse.quote: This becomes even more evident when another priest arises in the likeness of Melchizedek, who has become a priest, not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent, but by the power of an indestructible life. For it is witnessed of him, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Another priest arises in the likeness of Melchizedek” — and the word for another means another of a different kind, not merely one more of the same sort. This is not a successor. It is a different species of priest.

Then the contrast that is the heart of the chapter: “who has become a priest, not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent, but by the power of an indestructible life.”

The Greek behind “bodily descent” is literally a commandment of fleshly requirement — a rule about physical pedigree. That is what qualified a man under the old system: not his character, not his devotion, not his gifts, but his birth certificate. A godly Israelite from the wrong tribe could not serve; an indifferent one from the right family could.

Against that stands “the power of an indestructible life”. The word means undissolvable, incapable of being broken up. Not merely a life that happens to go on but one that cannot be ended — and the resurrection is behind the phrase. Death did its worst and could not dissolve it.

Set the two qualifications side by side and the difference is the whole argument. One priesthood rests on a document about ancestry; the other on a life that death could not destroy. The first is guaranteed by records that can be lost, as they were after the exile (Ezra 2:61–62). The second is guaranteed by an empty tomb.

“For it is witnessed of him” — and Psalm 110:4 is quoted for the third time in the letter. The writer keeps returning to it because the whole case rests on those seven words, and he wants his hearers to know them by heart.

“You are a priest forever.” Everything hangs on the middle word. A priest forever needs no successor, takes no holiday, and cannot be replaced by a better one.

verseByVerse.quote: For on the one hand, a former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness (for the law made nothing perfect); but on the other hand, a better hope is introduced, through which we draw near to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“A former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness.”

These are strong words about God’s own law, and they must be read exactly or they will be misread badly. The writer is not saying the law was a mistake, or evil, or contemptible. He has just said the people received it under the Levitical priesthood by divine arrangement.

“Weakness” and “uselessness” are judgements about capacity for a particular purpose. The law was perfectly effective at what it was given to do: it exposed sin, regulated a nation, and pointed forward. It was useless for making anybody perfect, which it never claimed to do. A thermometer is useless for heating a room, and the fault is not in the thermometer.

Hence the parenthesis, which is the plainest statement of it in Scripture: “(for the law made nothing perfect)”. Not nobody — nothing. In fourteen centuries the entire apparatus of priesthood, sacrifice and ceremony never brought one thing to completion.

“But on the other hand, a better hope is introduced.” The word “better” is the letter’s signature; it uses it thirteen times, more than the rest of the New Testament together. Better priest, better covenant, better promises, better sacrifices, better country.

And then the purpose clause, which is where the whole chapter has been going: “through which we draw near to God.”

That is the point of all of it — the genealogies, the tithes, the tribes, the oath. Not to win an argument about priesthood but to get people into the presence of God. The old system existed to manage distance: curtains, courts, and a single man admitted once a year. The new one exists to remove it.

“Draw near” is the same verb as 4:16 and it will return at 10:22. It is the letter’s word for what a Christian actually does, and everything else is scaffolding around it.

verseByVerse.quote: And it was not without an oath. For those who formerly became priests were made such without an oath, but this one was made a priest with an oath by the one who said to him: “The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind, ’You are a priest forever.’” This makes Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And it was not without an oath.” The writer returns to the argument he made about Abraham in chapter 6, and applies it now to the priesthood.

“Those who formerly became priests were made such without an oath.” And that is a striking observation, easily verified by anyone who goes and looks. The whole Levitical arrangement was instituted by command — Exodus and Leviticus are full of instructions about the priesthood, and God never once swears to it. He legislated it. He did not guarantee it on oath.

“But this one was made a priest with an oath… The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind.”

Psalm 110:4 again, and this time the writer quotes the clause he has previously left out. The psalm does not merely announce the priesthood; it records God swearing to it and declaring that he will not reverse the decision.

An arrangement made by command can be amended by a later command — and the Levitical system was in fact amended repeatedly and finally set aside. An arrangement established by the oath of God, who has already been said to find lying impossible (6:18), cannot be.

“This makes Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant.” The word is engyos, and it is a legal and commercial term found nowhere else in the New Testament: a surety, the person who stands behind an obligation with his own property and his own person. If the debtor fails, the guarantor pays.

Consider what that means here. A covenant has two parties, and covenants fail because one of them does — which is exactly what happened to the first one. Jesus is not the covenant’s administrator or its witness. He is the surety, and he stands behind it with himself.

Which means the new covenant cannot fail on our side, because our side has a guarantor who has already paid. The word appears once in the Bible, and it is the strongest security a first-century reader had a category for.

verseByVerse.quote: The former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever. Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office.”

Tradition counted around eighty high priests between Aaron and the destruction of the temple. Eighty men, eighty funerals, eighty consecrations. And the writer says the reason there were so many is stated plainly: death kept interrupting.

Picture what that meant for an ordinary Israelite. The man who represented you before God would one day be carried out, and somebody else would put on the robes. Whatever confidence you had in him died with him.

“But he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever.” The word for permanently means unchangeable, not passing to another — it was used of things that cannot be transferred. His office is not on loan and will never be handed on.

“Consequently” — and everything in the chapter now cashes out in one of the great verses of the Bible.

“He is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him.” The phrase can mean completely or forever, and the ambiguity is a gift: both are true. He saves entirely, leaving nothing unfinished, and he saves permanently, without expiry. Nothing in a person is beyond its reach and no stretch of time is outside it.

“Those who draw near” — the letter’s word again, and it is the only qualification named. Not those who understand, or who have never failed. Those who come.

“Since he always lives to make intercession for them.” And there is the ground, and rest on. What is Christ doing now? Hebrews answers: he is praying for his people, and he never stops.

That is a strange and steadying thing to hold on to. At three in the morning, when a Christian is too tired or too ashamed to pray for himself, there is somebody at the right hand of God who is praying for him and has not paused. The salvation reaches to the uttermost because the interceding does.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was indeed fitting that we should have such a high priest, holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens. He has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people, since he did this once for all when he offered up himself. For the law appoints men in their weakness as high priests, but the word of the oath, which came later than the law, appoints a Son who has been made perfect forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“It was indeed fitting that we should have such a high priest” — the word from 2:10 again. Not merely that we needed one but that it suited the character of God to provide him.

Five descriptions follow, and they move outward from his character to his location.

“Holy” — the word here is not the usual one for holiness but a term for devout, pious, wholly given to God; it describes his Godward disposition. “Innocent” — literally without evil, harmless, containing no malice. “Unstained” — the sacrificial word for an animal without defect.

“Separated from sinners” requires care, because it can be read to contradict everything the Gospels show. The man who was called a friend of tax collectors and sinners is not being described as aloof. The separation is moral and, since the ascension, positional — he was among sinners without becoming one, and is now “exalted above the heavens”.

Then verse 27 sets the two priesthoods side by side one last time, and the difference is in a single phrase. The old priests had to offer “daily… first for his own sins and then for those of the people”. Two problems: it never stopped, and he had to deal with himself first.

“Since he did this once for all when he offered up himself.” The phrase is ephapax — once, finally, never to be repeated; it is one of the letter’s great words and it will dominate chapters 9 and 10.

And the last three words are where the chapter arrives. Every other priest offered something else — a bull, a goat, a lamb. This one had nothing to bring but himself, and brought it. Priest and sacrifice in the same person, which no religious system had ever imagined.

“The law appoints men in their weakness… but the word of the oath, which came later than the law, appoints a Son.” The chapter closes on the two contrasts it has been building: weak men against a Son, and a temporary command against a later oath. Psalm 110 came after Sinai, and God does not swear to things he means to revise.
