The verse also settles a question that has divided Christians. If there is no longer any offering for sin, then whatever the church does when it gathers, it is not offering a sacrifice for sin. The New Testament knows sacrifices of praise and of doing good (13:15-16) and calls a Christian’s body a living sacrifice (Rom 12:1). It knows no repeatable offering for sin, and this verse is why.

With that the great doctrinal argument of the letter is complete. From here the writer turns to what his readers must do about it, and the next verse begins “therefore”.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–39 — Let Us Draw Near, Hold Fast, and Consider One Another
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Therefore, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus (v.19), by the new and living way opened through the curtain, that is, his flesh (v.20), and a great priest over God’s house (v.21) — let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, hearts sprinkled clean and bodies washed (v.22); let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful (v.23); and let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works (v.24), not neglecting to meet together as some do, but encouraging one another all the more as the Day draws near (v.25).

For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains (v.26), but a fearful expectation of judgement (v.27). Anyone setting aside Moses’ law died without mercy on two or three witnesses (v.28); how much worse for one who has trampled the Son of God, profaned the blood of the covenant and outraged the Spirit of grace (v.29)? For we know him who said, vengeance is mine, and the Lord will judge his people (v.30) — and it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God (v.31).

But recall the former days: after being enlightened you endured a hard struggle (v.32), publicly exposed to reproach, and partners with those so treated (v.33); you had compassion on prisoners and joyfully accepted the plundering of your property, knowing you had a better and abiding possession (v.34). So do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward (v.35); you have need of endurance, to receive what is promised (v.36). For yet a little while and the coming one will come (v.37); my righteous one shall live by faith, and if he shrinks back my soul has no pleasure in him (v.38). But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls (v.39).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Curtain Is His Flesh

The identification in verse 20 is startling and repays sitting with. The curtain was the barrier — the thing that kept people out — and the writer says the curtain is his flesh. Which means the way in was opened by the tearing of it: when Jesus died the temple veil was torn from top to bottom (Mark 15:38), an act done from above rather than below.

There is a further note the readers would have felt. The curtain was beautiful — blue and purple and scarlet, worked with cherubim. The barrier between God and man was not ugly. It was magnificent, and it had to be destroyed.

Note also what is not among the four qualifications of verse 22. There is no requirement of worthiness, no interval of preparation, no measure of progress. Every one is either an attitude of honesty or something Christ has already done — which is the point, because a throne you must qualify for is not a throne of grace. And the ground of holding fast in verse 23 is not our grip but his faithfulness: a man gritting his teeth relies on his own hold, and grips fail.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verses 32–34 are the most valuable historical paragraph in the letter, telling us what had actually happened to these people. The suffering came after the enlightenment — becoming Christians is what brought it on them. They were “publicly exposed”, a theatre word meaning made a spectacle of, in a culture where honour and shame were the currency of a life. They visited prisoners, which meant identifying yourself publicly with the crime. And they “joyfully accepted” the plundering of their property — not endured, not tolerated — while their houses were emptied, presumably by neighbours, with no legal recourse. They did it by knowing they owned something the mob could not carry.

Now: The fourth warning (vv.26–31) must be read with attention to the words chosen, because it has terrified people it was never aimed at. “Deliberately” stands first in the Greek and is a technical term: the law distinguished unintentional sin, for which sacrifice was provided (Lev 4), from sin done “with a high hand”, for which there was none (Num 15:30–31). Add “go on” (persisting) and “after receiving the knowledge of the truth” (with full information), and the sin in view is the informed, deliberate, persistent repudiation of Christ described in verse 29 as trampling him underfoot. It does not describe a Christian who has sinned badly or is losing a fight with a besetting sin — such a person has a sacrifice, and the whole letter urges him to come and use it.

Note finally how the chapter ends: as at 6:9, the writer follows his sternest warning by placing himself and his readers on the other side of it. Warning and assurance are not alternatives here; the warning is one of the means by which the assurance turns out to be true.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh, and since we have a great priest over the house of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Therefore, brothers” — and the letter turns. Nine chapters of argument now become three exhortations, and everything from here rests on what has been proved.

“Since we have confidence to enter the holy places.” The word is parresia, as at 4:16 — the free citizen’s right to speak openly. And the place named is the one the whole letter has been circling: the room behind the curtain, which one man entered once a year and everybody else never.

“By the blood of Jesus.” That is the ground, and it is the only one offered. Not by sincerity, not by improvement, not by a life that has earned an audience.

“By the new and living way that he opened for us.” The word for new here originally meant freshly slaughtered, and something of that lingers. And “living” is the arresting adjective: not a road but a way that is alive, because it is a person.

“Through the curtain, that is, through his flesh.”

The identification is startling and it repays sitting with. The curtain was the barrier — the thing that kept people out. And the writer says the curtain is his flesh.

Which means the way in was opened by the tearing of it. When Jesus died, the temple veil was torn from top to bottom (Mark 15:38), and the Gospels record it as an act done from above rather than below. His body was rent, and the barrier with it.

There is a further note in it that the readers would have felt. The curtain was beautiful — blue and purple and scarlet, worked with cherubim. The barrier between God and man was not ugly. It was magnificent, and it had to be destroyed.

“And since we have a great priest over the house of God.” The second ground: not only an open way but a man standing at the end of it who belongs to us. “Over the house” recalls 3:6, where Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son — and we are that house.

verseByVerse.quote: let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let us draw near.” The first of the three exhortations, and it is the letter’s central verb — the priestly word, used of what only priests could do, now commanded of everybody.

Four qualifications follow, and they divide into two pairs: two about the person coming, two about what has been done to him.

“With a true heart” — a genuine one, without pretence. This rules out the approach that keeps something back, and it also rules out coming in somebody else’s borrowed words. God is not interested in a performance at the throne.

“In full assurance of faith” — the same phrase as 6:11, meaning carried to complete conviction. Not certainty about oneself, which nobody has, but certainty about the ground just described: the blood, the way, the priest.

Then the second pair, and both verbs are passive — things done to us rather than by us.

“With our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience.” The image is the sprinkling that consecrated priests at their ordination (Exod 29:21), and the target is the conscience again — the thing 9:9 said the old sacrifices could not reach. What accuses a man on the inside has been dealt with, and that is why he can come with a true heart rather than a defended one.

“And our bodies washed with pure water.” Priests were also washed at their ordination, and most readers hear an allusion to baptism here as well. Whether or not the writer intended that, the pairing is deliberate: inward cleansing and outward, the whole person made fit.

Put the four together and notice what is not among them. There is no requirement of worthiness, no interval of preparation, no measure of progress. Every qualification is either an attitude of honesty or something Christ has already done — which is exactly the point, because a throne you must qualify for is not a throne of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering.” The second exhortation, and it is the one aimed most directly at these readers’ situation.

“The confession” is the word from 3:1 and 4:14 — what they had said publicly, probably at baptism, and were under pressure to unsay. In a hostile city a confession is not a private opinion; it is the thing that got their property confiscated.

“Hold fast” means grip, retain, do not let go. And “without wavering” is a single word meaning not leaning, not tilting — the picture is of something that stays upright rather than swaying between two positions.

Then the reason, and it is one short clause carrying the whole weight: “for he who promised is faithful.”

Read it carefully, because the logic is not the one we would supply. He does not say hold on because you are strong, or because you have held on so far, or because giving up would be shameful. The ground of our holding is his faithfulness.

That is the difference between Christian perseverance and mere determination. A man gritting his teeth is relying on his grip, and grips fail. A man holding fast because the promiser is faithful is relying on something outside himself, and the holding on is a response to reliability rather than a substitute for it.

Notice too what is held: the confession of our hope. Not of our feelings, which come and go, and not of our achievements. Hope is by definition about something not yet in hand, which is why holding it requires anything at all.

And this is the answer to the drift of 2:1. A congregation slipping away is not usually losing an argument; it is losing its grip in the dark. The writer does not give them a new argument. He points at the character of the one who made the promise, and tells them to hang on to that.

verseByVerse.quote: And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works.” The third exhortation, and it turns outward. The first two were about our approach to God; this one is about each other.

“Consider” is the verb from 3:1, where it was applied to Jesus — to fix the mind on, to study attentively. Here it is applied to other Christians. Working out how to help a particular person forward requires the same kind of attention as contemplating Christ, and the writer uses the same word for both.

“Stir up” is a startling choice. The noun is paroxysmos, from which we get paroxysm; it means a sharp provoking, an irritation. It is the word Luke uses of the bitter quarrel between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:39).

So the instruction is to provoke one another — and the only thing that redeems it is the object. Provoke, yes, but to love and good works. There is a kind of friction between Christians that is entirely legitimate: the friend who will not let you settle, whose example makes your comfort uncomfortable.

“Not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some.” And here is the first concrete symptom the letter has named. The drift of 2:1 and the dullness of 5:11 have a visible expression: people had stopped coming.

Note that it is called a habit. Not a decision, not a repudiation. A pattern that had established itself, which is exactly how drifting works.

And the reasons would have been good ones. Meeting was dangerous; assembling with Christians marked you out in a city that had already plundered their property. Staying away was prudent. The writer names it anyway, because the previous verses have just made attendance the mechanism of everything else — you cannot stir up one another, or be stirred, from a distance.

“But encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near.” The instinct under pressure is to withdraw and go quiet. The letter says the opposite: the nearer the Day and the harder the times, the more of this, not less.

verseByVerse.quote: For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins.”

The fourth warning, and it must be read with the same care as chapter 6 — and with attention to the words the writer actually chose.

“Deliberately” stands first in the Greek sentence, in the emphatic position. And the phrase is a technical one. The law distinguished sins committed unintentionally, for which sacrifice was provided (Lev 4), from sin done “with a high hand”, for which there was no offering at all and the sinner was cut off (Num 15:30–31). The writer is using that category, and his readers would have recognised it instantly.

“Go on sinning” is a present participle: continuing, persisting. Not a fall but a settled course.

“After receiving the knowledge of the truth” — with full information. This is not the sin of the ignorant or the deceived.

Put those together and the sin in view is specific: the informed, deliberate, persistent repudiation of Christ by someone who knows exactly what he is walking away from. Verse 29 will describe it in the plainest terms — trampling the Son of God underfoot.

“There no longer remains a sacrifice for sins.” And the logic is the same as verse 18, running the other way. There is one sacrifice, offered once. A person who rejects it has not exhausted a supply; he has refused the only one there is, and there is no second provision behind it.

This should be said plainly for the comfort of the anxious, because these verses have terrified people they were never aimed at. The passage does not describe a Christian who has sinned badly, or repeatedly, or who is fighting a besetting sin and losing. Such a person has a sacrifice, and the whole letter has been urging him to come and use it. It describes someone who has looked at the sacrifice and trampled on it.

“But a fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire.” The language is Isaiah’s (Isa 26:11), and the word for adversaries makes the point: this is what awaits enemies, not stumbling sons.

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has outraged the Spirit of grace? For we know him who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.” And again, “The Lord will judge his people.” It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The argument runs again from lesser to greater, as at 2:2.

“Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses.” That is Deuteronomy 17:6, and the offence in view there is idolatry — going and serving other gods. The penalty was death, and the safeguard was witnesses.

“How much worse punishment, do you think…” The writer puts it as a question and invites his readers to do the arithmetic themselves.

Three descriptions follow, and they escalate.

“Has trampled underfoot the Son of God” — not merely rejected but treated with contempt, walked on. “Has profaned the blood of the covenant” — the verb means to treat as common, to reckon something holy as ordinary. “And has outraged the Spirit of grace” — insulted, treated with insolence.

The phrase “by which he was sanctified” has been much debated, since it appears to describe the apostate as having been sanctified by the blood. It most likely means set apart in the external sense — he belonged to the covenant community and was marked out by it, as Israel was sanctified at Sinai. That is consistent with everything the letter says elsewhere, and with the field in 6:7–8 that drank the same rain.

“For we know him who said, Vengeance is mine.” Two quotations from Deuteronomy 32, and the second is the sharper: “The Lord will judge his people.” Not the nations. His people. Belonging to the covenant community is not a shelter from God’s judgement; it is the reason judgement begins there (cf. 1 Pet 4:17).

“It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.”

And note the phrase, because it is the letter’s own and it cuts both ways. To fall away is to fall away from the living God (3:12) — and there is nowhere to fall except into his hands. The same hands are the only refuge and the only danger, and which they are depends entirely on how a man comes.

verseByVerse.quote: But recall the former days when, after you were enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings, sometimes being publicly exposed to reproach and affliction, and sometimes being partners with those so treated. For you had compassion on those in prison, and you joyfully accepted the plundering of your property, since you knew that you yourselves had a better possession and an abiding one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But recall the former days” — and the tone changes completely. Having brought them to the edge, the writer turns and reminds them who they are.

This is the most valuable historical paragraph in the letter, because it tells us what had actually happened to these people.

“After you were enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings.” The word for struggle is athlesis, the athletic contest word. And note the timing: the suffering came after the light, not before. Becoming Christians is what brought it on them.

“Sometimes being publicly exposed to reproach and affliction.” The verb is a theatre word — made a spectacle of, put on a stage. Public humiliation, in a culture where honour and shame were the currency of a life.

“And sometimes being partners with those so treated.” Which took its own kind of courage. It is one thing to be dragged out yourself; it is another to walk over and stand beside somebody who has been, when you could have stayed indoors.

“For you had compassion on those in prison.” Visiting a prisoner in that world meant identifying yourself publicly with his crime, and prisoners depended on visitors for food. These people went.

“And you joyfully accepted the plundering of your property.”

Read that twice. Not endured. Not tolerated. Joyfully accepted — while their houses were being emptied, presumably by neighbours, with no legal recourse whatever.

“Since you knew that you yourselves had a better possession and an abiding one.” And there is how they did it. Not by stoicism or by pretending the loss was small. By knowing they owned something the mob could not reach and could not carry.

The word “abiding” is the letter’s word for what lasts, set against everything that wears out like a garment (1:11). These people had once made that calculation under real pressure and come out singing — which is precisely why the writer reminds them. He is not asking them to become something new. He is asking them to be what they already were.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward. For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Therefore do not throw away your confidence.”

The verb is deliberate and slightly shocking. Not “do not lose” it, as though it might slip out of a pocket. To throw away is an act — you do it on purpose, the way a soldier throws away a shield to run faster.

And “confidence” is parresia, the same word as verse 19 and 4:16: the boldness to speak, the freedom to come. What they are in danger of discarding is not a mood but their access.

The word was also used of the frankness that could get a man into trouble in a public assembly. There is a version of quietness that looks like humility and is actually the shield going over the wall.

“Which has a great reward.” The writer is not embarrassed by the motive. He has told them their possession is better and abiding (v.34), and here he says the boldness itself is worth keeping because of what it earns. Reward-language runs through this letter (11:6, 11:26) and it is never treated as a lower motive.

“For you have need of endurance.” A plain sentence, and notice what it concedes. Not need of better arguments, or clearer teaching, or a fresh experience. Endurance — hypomone, remaining under a weight without buckling.

That is the writer’s diagnosis after ten chapters of theology, and it is a humbling one for anyone who assumes that people leave the faith because they have run out of reasons. These readers had the reasons. What they were short of was staying power.

“So that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised.” And note the order. Doing comes first and receiving after — not because the promise is earned, but because it lies at the end of a road that must actually be walked. Endurance is not waiting; it is continuing to obey while nothing visible changes.

verseByVerse.quote: For, “Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay; but my righteous one shall live by faith, and if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer quotes Habakkuk, and he has chosen the passage with care, because Habakkuk is the prophet of waiting. His book opens with the complaint: how long, O LORD, and you will not hear? The answer he received was that the vision awaits its appointed time; if it seems slow, wait for it (Hab 2:3).

“Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay.” The Greek reads literally “a little while, how little, how little” — a doubling that presses the shortness. And the writer has adjusted the prophet’s “it” to “he”: what is coming is not an event but a person.

“But my righteous one shall live by faith.” It is the sentence that changed Luther’s life and Paul builds two letters on it (Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11). Hebrews uses it differently, and the difference is instructive.

Paul takes it to answer the question how is a man justified — by faith, not works. Hebrews takes it to answer how does a man keep going — by faith, not sight. The emphasis here falls on live: the righteous man does not merely begin by faith, he lives by it, day after day, and the whole of chapter 11 is about to illustrate what that looks like over a lifetime.

“And if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.” The verb means to draw back, to withdraw — it was used of furling a sail and of a man shrinking from danger. Paul uses it of himself at Miletus: I did not shrink from declaring the whole counsel of God (Acts 20:27).

And the contrast is exact. Faith goes forward when it cannot see; shrinking back is what faith looks like when it fails. The wilderness generation shrank back at the border of a good land, and it is the same failure of nerve.

“My soul has no pleasure in him” is a restrained way of saying something severe, and its restraint is characteristic of Scripture at its most serious. It is not rage. It is the withdrawal of delight, which from God is worse.

verseByVerse.quote: But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.”

The chapter that contains the letter’s most frightening warning ends with the writer putting himself and his readers firmly on the right side of it — and the placing is deliberate.

“We” — he includes himself, as he has in every warning since 2:1. And “are not of those” is a statement of category, not of achievement. He is not saying we have performed better. He is saying we belong to a different kind.

This is how the warnings in Hebrews are meant to work, and the pattern repays learning, because it recurs. The writer describes the danger in the strongest terms available, and then tells his readers he does not believe it applies to them — exactly as he did at 6:9 after the harshest passage in the letter. Warning and assurance are not alternatives here. The warning is one of the means by which the assurance turns out to be true.

“Shrink back and are destroyed” — the word means ruin, loss, the same root as the perdition of 2 Peter and Philippians 3:19. Set against it is “preserve their souls”, literally the gaining or keeping of the soul, an idiom for coming through alive.

And the two categories are defined by one thing only, which the writer names last: faith. Not endurance, though he has just demanded it; not good works, though he has commended theirs. Faith is what distinguishes those who arrive from those who turn back.

Which is exactly why the next chapter is what it is. Having said that the difference between destruction and preservation is faith, the writer immediately defines it — and then spends forty verses producing a crowd of people who had it, so that a struggling congregation could see what the word looks like when it is worn by real men and women over a lifetime.

10.text: <sup>1</sup>For since the law has but a shadow of the good things to come instead of the true form of these realities, it can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered every year, make perfect those who draw near.<sup>2</sup>Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, since the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins?<sup>3</sup>But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year.<sup>4</sup>For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.<sup>5</sup>Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said, “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me;<sup>6</sup>in burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure.<sup>7</sup>Then I said, ’Behold, I have come to do your will, O God, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book.’”<sup>8</sup>When he said above, “You have neither desired nor taken pleasure in sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings and sin offerings” (these are offered according to the law),<sup>9</sup>then he added, “Behold, I have come to do your will.” He does away with the first in order to establish the second.<sup>10</sup>And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.<sup>11</sup>And every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins.<sup>12</sup>But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God,<sup>13</sup>waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool for his feet.<sup>14</sup>For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.<sup>15</sup>And the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us; for after saying,<sup>16</sup>“This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws on their hearts, and write them on their minds,”<sup>17</sup>then he adds, “I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more.”<sup>18</sup>Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.<sup>19</sup>Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus,<sup>20</sup>by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh,<sup>21</sup>and since we have a great priest over the house of God,<sup>22</sup>let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.<sup>23</sup>Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.<sup>24</sup>And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works,<sup>25</sup>not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near.<sup>26</sup>For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins,<sup>27</sup>but a fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries.<sup>28</sup>Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses.<sup>29</sup>How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has outraged the Spirit of grace?<sup>30</sup>For we know him who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.” And again, “The Lord will judge his people.”<sup>31</sup>It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.<sup>32</sup>But recall the former days when, after you were enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings,<sup>33</sup>sometimes being publicly exposed to reproach and affliction, and sometimes being partners with those so treated.<sup>34</sup>For you had compassion on those in prison, and you joyfully accepted the plundering of your property, since you knew that you yourselves had a better possession and an abiding one.<sup>35</sup>Therefore do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward.<sup>36</sup>For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised.<sup>37</sup>For, “Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay;<sup>38</sup>but my righteous one shall live by faith, and if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.”<sup>39</sup>But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.

11.title: By Faith: The Great Cloud of Witnesses
11.overview:
Chapter 11 is one of the most beloved passages in all of Scripture — the great gallery of faith, a sweeping movement through salvation history that shows what it looks like to live by trust in what is not yet visible. The writer has spent ten chapters making the theological case for the all-sufficiency of Jesus; now he demonstrates it experimentally, showing that the saints of the Old Testament were sustained through their entire lives by faith in the promises of God — promises they received, embraced, and died without fully receiving. They were looking forward to what we have received. Their faith and ours are one continuous movement toward the one promised city.

The definition of faith in verse 1 is not a philosophical proposition but a practical description: “the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.” Faith is not a leap in the dark or an act of wishful thinking; it is the settled confidence that what God has promised is more real than what can be seen and touched, precisely because it is grounded in God’s character and sworn by his oath. It is, as the writer has shown in chapters 1–10, a reasonable response to the evidence: the evidence of the Son, the better covenant, the better sacrifice, the permanent intercession.

The chapter’s theological climax comes at the end: “And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised, since God had provided something better for us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect.” The Old Testament saints were not left behind. They are not inferior. They are incomplete without us — and we are incomplete without them. The entire company of the redeemed, across all the ages, will together receive the fullness of the promise. This is the most moving vision of the solidarity of the saints in all of Scripture.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — By Faith: Title Deeds and Tents
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen (v.1), by which the people of old were commended (v.2) — and by which we understand that the universe was made by God’s word, so that the visible did not come from the visible (v.3). By faith Abel offered a better sacrifice and still speaks though dead (v.4); Enoch was taken without seeing death, commended as having pleased God (v.5) — and without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever draws near must believe that he is and that he rewards those who seek him (v.6). By faith Noah built an ark for events as yet unseen (v.7).

By faith Abraham obeyed and went out not knowing where he was going (v.8), living in tents in the land of promise with Isaac and Jacob (v.9), looking for the city with foundations whose builder is God (v.10). By faith Sarah received power to conceive, considering him faithful who had promised (v.11), so that from one man as good as dead came descendants like the stars and the sand (v.12).

These all died in faith without receiving the promises, having greeted them from afar as strangers and exiles (v.13) — and people who speak so are seeking a homeland (v.14); had they meant the land they left, they could have returned (v.15), but they desire a better, heavenly country, so God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared them a city (v.16). By faith Abraham offered Isaac (v.17), of whom it was said the offspring would be named (v.18), reckoning that God could raise him (v.19). By faith Isaac blessed (v.20), Jacob worshipped over his staff (v.21), and Joseph gave directions about his bones (v.22).
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith as a Title Deed

Verse 1 is not quite a definition — the writer says what faith does. Hypostasis means that which stands under, a substructure; the word was used at 1:3 of the very being of God, and in the papyri it appears in property documents for a title deed — the paper establishing a claim to something not yet held. A man with a deed to a house he has never seen owns it, and behaves accordingly. Elenchos is a courtroom word: proof, the evidence that settles a case.

Both guard against a misunderstanding that has done real damage. Faith here is not a leap in the dark or believing without grounds, because its ground is not the strength of the believing but the reliability of the promiser (10:23). And note that not one person in this gallery is commended for holding an opinion. Every single one is commended for something they did that made no sense apart from a word from God.

The chapter starts with creation for a reason (v.3): nobody watched it, there were no witnesses and there could not be, so everyone who believes the world was made does so on testimony rather than observation. The readers already order their whole understanding of reality around an event none of them saw. And if the visible came out of the invisible, the invisible is the more solid of the two — which is what Moses acts on at verse 27.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The irony of verses 9–10 is meant to be felt. Abraham arrived in the land of promise and remained a stranger in it; the only ground he ever bought was a cave to bury his wife in (Gen 23). Three generations lived under canvas in the country God had given them, and none of the three saw it kept. He could live in the temporary because he expected the permanent — a tent is the least permanent structure a man can live in, and foundations are the part of a building that does not move.

Now: Verse 16 contains one of the most moving sentences in Scripture. God calls himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob — three men who lived in tents and died holding nothing — and is not ashamed of the association. People visibly waiting for another country do not embarrass him; it is the ones who have settled here who make the title awkward. Note too the generosity of verse 11: Sarah laughed at the promise and then denied laughing (Gen 18:12–15), and Hebrews says by faith. God commends what he sees underneath a mixed performance. And verse 19 shows faith reasoning rather than blind — Abraham considered that God could raise the dead, inferring a resurrection for which there was no precedent in the world, from the character of God alone. He told the servants “we will come again to you” (Gen 22:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen. For by it the people of old received their commendation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.”

It is not quite a definition. The writer is not saying what faith is in the abstract; he is saying what faith does, and the two nouns repay pressing.

“Assurance” is hypostasis — literally that which stands under, a substructure. The same word was used at 1:3 of the very being of God. In the papyri it appears in property documents for a title deed, the paper that establishes a claim to something you do not yet hold.

That is a remarkable thing to say about faith. It does not merely wish for the things hoped for; it gives them a footing in the present. A man with a title deed to a house he has never seen owns it, and behaves accordingly.

“Conviction” is elenchos, a word from the law courts — proof, evidence, the demonstration that settles a case. Faith functions as evidence of what cannot be seen.

Both words guard against a misunderstanding that has done real damage. Faith in Hebrews is not a leap in the dark, and it is not believing without grounds. It is the settled confidence that treats God’s word as the evidence it is — because the ground of faith is not the strength of the believing but the reliability of the promiser (10:23).

Note also what faith is directed toward: things hoped for and things not seen. Both are about the invisible and the future, which is exactly the difficulty these readers were in. They could see the temple, the neighbours, the empty houses. What they could not see was the thing they had been promised.

“For by it the people of old received their commendation.” The word means to be witnessed to, well spoken of — and it recurs through the chapter (vv. 4, 5, 39). God himself is the one bearing witness. The whole gallery that follows exists to show that this is what he approves.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God.”

The first example is not a person, and the choice is deliberate. Before Abel, before Noah, before Abraham, the writer begins with the whole congregation and something every one of them believes.

And note the pairing: faith and understand. They are not opposites here. Faith is presented as the faculty by which something is genuinely known — not a substitute for understanding but the means of it.

“The universe was created by the word of God.” Which is exactly how Genesis tells it: God said, and it was. Nothing was worked with, shaped, or wrestled into form. He spoke.

“So that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible.” The visible world does not have a visible origin. Trace it back as far as you like and you do not arrive at earlier stuff; you arrive at a word.

Why start here? Because the chapter is about acting on the strength of what cannot be seen, and creation is the first and largest instance. Nobody watched it happen. There were no witnesses, and there is no possibility of any. Every person who believes the world was made does so on the strength of testimony rather than observation.

So the writer establishes at the outset that this is not a strange way to hold anything. His readers already order their whole understanding of reality around an event none of them saw — and he is about to ask them to keep ordering their lives around a promise they cannot see either.

There is a further thread here that runs through the chapter. If the visible came out of the invisible, then the invisible is the more solid of the two. That is the conviction Moses will act on when he endures “as seeing him who is invisible” (v.27), and the one these readers needed when their visible property was being carried out of their houses.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain, through which he was commended as righteous, God commending him by accepting his gifts. And through his faith, though he died, he still speaks. By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death, and he was not found, because God had taken him. Now before he was taken he was commended as having pleased God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain.” Genesis does not say why Abel’s was accepted and his brother’s refused; it records the fact and moves on. The writer supplies the reason: faith.

Not the material of the offering, then, and not the technique. Two men brought what they had, and God saw what was underneath it. That is a sobering thing to know about worship, and it is the earliest instance in Scripture of the principle this letter keeps applying: the same act performed by two people is not the same act.

“Through his faith, though he died, he still speaks.” A beautiful sentence, and it works two ways. In Genesis it is Abel’s blood that cries out from the ground (Gen 4:10); here it is his faith that goes on speaking. He is the first man in the Bible to die and the first to be murdered, and he is still saying something to a congregation four thousand years later.

Notice about the whole chapter. Everyone in it is dead, and every one of them is still talking.

“By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death.” The shortest biography in Genesis: he walked with God, and he was not, for God took him (Gen 5:24). In a chapter that lists the seventh son, the years, and the death of every generation, one man has no death recorded.

“Before he was taken he was commended as having pleased God.” The Greek Old Testament renders “walked with God” as “pleased God”, which is where the writer gets the phrase — and it supplies the hinge into verse 6.

Set the two men side by side and the chapter has already made an important point. Abel died young and violently; Enoch did not die at all. Faith produced opposite outcomes in the first two examples, and both are commended. Anyone reading this chapter as a list of what faith gets you has been warned in the first two verses of the gallery.

verseByVerse.quote: And without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And without faith it is impossible to please him.”

The word is impossible again — the letter’s absolute, used of restoring apostates (6:4), of God lying (6:18), and of bulls and goats taking away sins (10:4). It is not that faithless obedience is inferior. It cannot please him at all.

That should be allowed to land, because it cuts against a very natural assumption. A person may live decently, give generously, and behave better than most of the congregation, and none of it registers as pleasing God if it is not done in faith. Paul says the same thing from the other side: whatever does not proceed from faith is sin (Rom 14:23).

The reason is not arbitrary. To do good without trusting God is to treat him as somebody to be managed rather than believed — and no relationship can be pleased by a partner who does not take the other at his word.

Then the two things anyone drawing near must believe, and they are strikingly modest.

“That he exists.” Not a developed doctrine of God. That he is there.

“And that he rewards those who seek him.” That he is worth approaching — that the seeking is not into an empty room.

Notice that the second is the harder of the two. A great many people believe God exists and behave as though seeking him were pointless; the practical atheism of the half-believing is not a denial of God’s existence but a settled expectation that nothing will come of approaching him. Hebrews says faith is precisely the confidence that something will.

And the reward-language should not be apologised for. It runs through the chapter — Moses was looking to the reward (v.26), the patriarchs to a city (v.10). Seeking God for what he gives is only mercenary if what he gives is something other than himself. It is not.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Noah, being warned by God concerning events as yet unseen, in reverent fear constructed an ark for the saving of his household. By this he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“By faith Noah, being warned by God concerning events as yet unseen, in reverent fear constructed an ark.”

Everything in this verse turns on the phrase about the unseen. Noah was told about something for which there was no evidence whatever — and if the world before the flood was as Scripture suggests, quite possibly about rain he had never watched fall.

“In reverent fear” is one word meaning godly caution. It is the same disposition credited to Christ at 5:7. Noah took God seriously, which is the whole of his commendation.

“Constructed an ark.” And here is where faith becomes visible. It was not a private conviction; it was a very large wooden object in a field, taking decades, in full view of neighbours who had every reason to think him mad.

That is what this chapter means by faith throughout, and state it plainly plainly because the word has softened in modern use. Not one person in this gallery is commended for holding an opinion. Every single one is commended for something they did that made no sense apart from a word from God.

“For the saving of his household.” The obedience of one man carried seven other people through. It is the same pattern as Rahab in verse 31, and it should be noticed by anyone whose family is watching them believe.

“By this he condemned the world.” Not by preaching at it, though Peter calls him a herald of righteousness (2 Pet 2:5). By building. A man taking God at his word in public passes a verdict on everyone who has heard the same word and done nothing — not by criticising them but simply by acting as though it were true.

“And became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.” The phrase is Paul’s, and it is placed here on a man who lived before Abraham, before the law, before circumcision. The righteousness that comes by faith is not a New Testament invention. It is how it has always worked.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going. By faith he went to live in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise. For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called… and he went out, not knowing where he was going.”

That last clause is one of the great descriptions of faith in Scripture, and the order of events is the point. He obeyed first and found out afterwards. God said go, and did not say where until he had gone.

Consider what it cost in that world. A man of sixty-five leaving Ur — a city with law, water, streets, and family — for an unnamed destination, with no map, no contract, and no possibility of verifying anything he had been told. Security in that culture was land and kin, and he left both.

“By faith he went to live in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, living in tents.”

Here is the sharper irony, and the writer means it to be felt. He arrived, and he was still a stranger. The land was promised to him and he never owned a field in it — the only ground he ever bought was a cave to bury his wife in (Gen 23). He lived in a tent for a hundred years in the country God had given him.

“With Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise.” Three generations under canvas. The son and the grandson inherited the promise and the tent together, and none of the three saw it kept.

“For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations.”

And there is the explanation, in the contrast between a tent and a city with foundations. A tent is the least permanent structure a man can live in — pegs and cloth, moved every season. Foundations are the opposite: the part of a building that does not move.

Abraham could live in the temporary because he was expecting the permanent. That is the logic of the whole chapter and it is the answer to the readers’ situation: people whose houses had been emptied, told about a man who never had a house and did not mind, because he was waiting for something with foundations.

“Whose designer and builder is God.” The words are an architect’s and a craftsman’s. Abraham never saw the city; he did know who was building it.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, even when she was past the age, since she considered him faithful who had promised. Therefore from one man, and him as good as dead, were born descendants as many as the stars of heaven and as many as the innumerable grains of sand by the seashore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, even when she was past the age.”

The commendation is generous, and any reader of Genesis will feel the generosity. Sarah laughed when she overheard the promise, and then denied laughing (Gen 18:12–15). She had earlier arranged a substitute in Hagar rather than wait. Her faith was not straightforward.

And Hebrews says: by faith. This is one of the clearest instances in Scripture of God commending what he sees underneath a mixed performance. He is not describing her as she behaved on her worst afternoon. He is describing what was actually there, and it was genuine.

“Since she considered him faithful who had promised.” There is the thing itself, and it is the same phrase as 10:23 — he who promised is faithful. Faith in this chapter is repeatedly a judgement about the character of the promiser rather than a feeling about the promise.

“Therefore from one man, and him as good as dead…” The phrase is blunt and Paul uses it too (Rom 4:19). A hundred-year-old body and a ninety-year-old womb, and the writer does not soften either.

That is important to the argument, because faith here is not optimism about the possible. Abraham and Sarah were not hoping for a favourable outcome within the range of nature. The situation was, humanly, closed — and the New Testament is careful to say so rather than pretend the odds were merely long.

“Were born descendants as many as the stars of heaven and as the grains of sand.” The two images are God’s own from the Genesis promises, and they were given to a childless man on a particular night, when he was taken outside and told to look up (Gen 15:5).

From one man as good as dead, a nation. And the readers of this letter were the proof — they were the sand, sitting in a room somewhere, hearing about the night their ancestor was told to count stars.

verseByVerse.quote: These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar, and having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. For people who speak thus make it clear that they are seeking a homeland. If they had been thinking of that land from which they had gone out, they would have had opportunity to return. But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer pauses the roll-call to say what all of them had in common, and it is not what a modern reader expects from a chapter about faith.

“These all died in faith, not having received the things promised.”

Read that against any account of faith that measures it by results. Every one of them died without getting it. Abraham never owned the land, never saw the nation, never met the offspring in whom all families would be blessed. He got Isaac and a burial cave.

“But having seen them and greeted them from afar.” The image is of travellers sighting a country from the deck of a ship and waving at a shore they will not reach on this voyage. They saw it. They were glad. They did not land.

“And having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth.” That is Abraham’s own description of himself when he came to buy the burial cave: I am a sojourner and foreigner among you (Gen 23:4).

“For people who speak thus make it clear that they are seeking a homeland.” The writer listens to how they talked and draws a conclusion from it. A man who calls himself a stranger has told you he belongs somewhere else.

Then verse 15 closes the obvious escape: “If they had been thinking of that land from which they had gone out, they would have had opportunity to return.” Ur was still there. The road ran both ways, and nobody was stopping them. Their homesickness was not for anywhere they had left.

“But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one.” The letter’s word again: better.

“Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God.” And that is one of the most moving sentences in Scripture. He calls himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob — three men who lived in tents and died holding nothing — and the writer says he is not embarrassed by the association. People who are visibly waiting for another country do not embarrass him. It is the ones who have settled here who make the title awkward.

“For he has prepared for them a city.” The reason he is not ashamed is that their hope is not a fantasy. He has actually built the thing.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac, and he who had received the promises was in the act of offering up his only son, of whom it was said, “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.” He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac.” Genesis 22, the hardest chapter in the Old Testament, and the writer takes it as the summit of Abraham’s faith rather than as a problem to be explained.

“He who had received the promises was in the act of offering up his only son… of whom it was said, Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.”

The writer sets out the contradiction deliberately, because it is the point. Everything God had promised depended on this boy. He was the promise, in a body. And God told Abraham to kill him.

So the test was not merely whether Abraham loved God more than his son, terrible as that is. It was whether he would obey a command that appeared to destroy the promise it came from. He was being asked to trust God against God.

“He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead.”

“Considered” is a reckoning word — he worked it out. This was not blind obedience or a suspension of thought. Abraham reasoned: the promise runs through Isaac; God does not lie; therefore if Isaac dies, God will raise him. It is arithmetic, and it is the only arithmetic that fits both facts.

And it is remarkable, because no one had ever been raised from the dead. There was no precedent in the world for what Abraham concluded God would do. He inferred the resurrection from the character of God alone.

Genesis records the conclusion in his own words, when he tells the servants to wait: “I and the boy will go over there and worship and come again to you” (Gen 22:5). He said we.

“From which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.” The word is parabole — in a parable. Isaac was as good as dead and came back down the mountain alive, and the whole episode is a picture: a father, an only son, wood carried up a hill, and a substitute provided by God at the last moment. Abraham named the place “the LORD will provide”, and two thousand years later, on a hill in the same region, he did.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Isaac invoked future blessings on Jacob and Esau. By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, bowing in worship over the head of his staff. By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave directions concerning his bones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three men in three verses, and what unites them is easily missed: all three acts of faith are performed by dying men about a future they will not see.

“By faith Isaac invoked future blessings on Jacob and Esau.” and remember how that scene actually went. Isaac was blind, deceived by his wife and younger son, and intended the blessing for Esau. He was, in the plainest terms, taken in.

Yet when he discovers the deception, he trembles violently and then says of Jacob: “yes, and he shall be blessed” (Gen 27:33). That is the moment Hebrews commends. Isaac recognised that God’s purpose had gone through his own mistake, and he did not try to undo it.

“By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph.” Another old blind man, and another crossing of hands — Jacob deliberately gave the greater blessing to the younger, over Joseph’s objection (Gen 48:14–19). The man who had stolen a blessing by deceit gives one away, at the end, by the same principle he had once tried to force.

“Bowing in worship over the head of his staff.” The detail is tender. An old man too weak to stand unsupported, leaning on the stick he had carried since he crossed the Jordan with nothing (Gen 32:10), worshipping.

“By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus and gave directions concerning his bones.”

This is the most striking of the three. Joseph was the second man in Egypt, with a palace, a title and a family established in the best land of the country. Nothing in his circumstances suggested that his descendants would ever leave, and the exodus was three hundred years away.

And he made them swear to carry his coffin out when they went. He would not be embalmed into an Egyptian tomb, however grand. His faith took the form of a funeral instruction — a set of bones in a box, sitting in Egypt for centuries as a standing statement that this was not home.

They kept the promise. Moses took the bones (Exod 13:19), and they were buried at Shechem after the conquest (Josh 24:32). The box travelled forty years in the wilderness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–40 — The Turn: Some Were Tortured
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
By faith Moses was hidden three months by parents unafraid of the king’s edict (v.23); grown, he refused to be called Pharaoh’s daughter’s son (v.24), choosing mistreatment with God’s people over the fleeting pleasures of sin (v.25), counting the reproach of Christ greater wealth than Egypt’s treasures, looking to the reward (v.26). By faith he left Egypt unafraid, enduring as seeing him who is invisible (v.27), and kept the Passover and sprinkled the blood (v.28).

By faith the people crossed the Red Sea, while the Egyptians attempting it drowned (v.29); the walls of Jericho fell after seven days (v.30); and Rahab the prostitute did not perish, having welcomed the spies (v.31). Time would fail to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel and the prophets (v.32), who conquered kingdoms, stopped lions’ mouths (v.33), quenched fire, escaped the sword, were made strong out of weakness (v.34).

Women received back their dead — and some were tortured, refusing release, to rise to a better life (v.35); others suffered mocking, flogging, chains (v.36); they were stoned, sawn in two, killed with the sword, wandering in skins of sheep and goats, destitute and afflicted (v.37) — of whom the world was not worthy — in deserts and caves (v.38). And all these, commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised (v.39), since God had provided something better for us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect (v.40).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Chapter Turns Over Mid-Verse

The most important structural feature of Hebrews 11 is the break inside verse 35. Up to “women received back their dead”, faith conquers kingdoms, shuts lions’ mouths, quenches fire and raises the dead. From “some were tortured”, the same faith is beaten to death on a frame, sawn in two, and left wandering in goatskins.

And the same word does both halves: they were tortured, refusing release, so that they might rise again — resurrection, the very thing the women received. Some got their dead back by it; some died for it. Identical faith, opposite outcomes, and both commended.

This is the paragraph the letter’s readers most needed, and it is the answer to every account of faith measured by results. A congregation whose property had been plundered could read the first half and wonder why their faith had produced no such deliverance. The second half says: it produced these people too. And in the middle of the squalor the writer interrupts himself with the great reversal — of whom the world was not worthy. The world looked at men in goatskins sleeping in caves and reckoned them worthless; God’s verdict is that the world was not good enough for them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Look at the six names in verse 32, because they are not the ones we would have chosen. Gideon demanded signs with a fleece; Barak would not go to battle unless a woman came too; Samson’s life was a catalogue of appetite; Jephthah made a terrible vow; David was an adulterer and a murderer; Samuel’s sons took bribes. The readers knew those stories far better than we do, and the writer puts them in the roll anyway — which tells you what the roll measures. Not achievement, and certainly not consistency, but the bare fact of taking God at his word in the middle of lives that were often a mess. Note too “were made strong out of weakness”: a passive verb, locating the strength somewhere other than in them.

Now: Three details repay carrying away. At the Red Sea the Egyptians did precisely what Israel did and it killed them — so the crossing was not a technique, and the chapter’s consistent claim is that the same act performed by two people is not the same act. At Jericho, nothing whatever happened on days one to six: faith often looks foolish for a period before it looks like anything, and the seventh day is the only one anybody remembers.

Rahab keeps her description — the writer does not call her the innkeeper — placed immediately after Moses, the only Gentile in the chapter and one of two women, who ended in the genealogy of Christ (Matt 1:5). Finally, verse 40 puts the readers where they had entirely failed to see themselves: drifting back toward the era these giants had lived in and longed to escape, while the whole gallery died waiting for what this discouraged little congregation actually possessed.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict. By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking to the reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents.”

The first act of faith in the Moses section is not his. It belongs to a mother and father defying a royal edict with a baby in a basket. “They were not afraid of the king’s edict” — and Exodus tells us the midwives feared God rather than Pharaoh, which is the same calculation.

“By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter.”

Weigh what was refused. Whatever his exact standing, he was raised in the royal household of the greatest power on earth, with its education, wealth and prospects — Stephen says he was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians (Acts 7:22). He walked away from it at forty.

“Choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin.”

The verb is a choosing word: he weighed two options and took one. And the two adjectives do all the work. The pleasures were real — the writer does not pretend Egypt was miserable — but fleeting, lasting a season. Set against them was mistreatment, which was also real, and permanent company: with the people of God.

That is the calculation this chapter keeps making, and it is not asceticism. It is arithmetic about duration.

“He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt.” A startling phrase, since Moses lived thirteen centuries early. It most likely means the reproach borne by God’s anointed people, and so by the Anointed One with whom they are identified — the same disgrace, in a different century.

“Greater wealth” is a deliberately commercial word, set against the literal treasures of the richest kingdom in the world. Moses did not weigh spiritual benefit against material loss. He weighed one wealth against another and concluded that reproach was the better asset.

“For he was looking to the reward.” The reason he could count that way, and it is verse 6 again. He was not being noble. He was looking at a figure the Egyptians could not see.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king, for he endured as seeing him who is invisible. By faith he kept the Passover and sprinkled the blood, so that the Destroyer of the firstborn might not touch them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king.”

There is a difficulty here worth naming, since Exodus says Moses fled to Midian because he was afraid (Exod 2:14). The likeliest reading is that this refers to the exodus itself rather than the flight — the writer follows the order of events, and the Passover comes in the next verse. Others take it as describing the settled disposition of a life rather than one bad afternoon. Either way, Hebrews is not rewriting the history; it is characterising a man.

“For he endured as seeing him who is invisible.”

It is the finest sentence in the chapter, and the paradox is deliberate. Seeing the invisible — the writer puts two words together that cannot go together, in order to say what faith actually does.

And it connects back to verse 3. If the visible world was made out of what cannot be seen, then the invisible is the more solid of the two, and a man who reckons with it is not being fanciful but realistic. Moses stood in front of the most visible power on earth, unimpressed, because he was looking at somebody else in the room.

“Endured” is the word from 10:36 — remaining under weight. That is what the seeing produced: not a mystical experience but forty years of staying put.

“By faith he kept the Passover and sprinkled the blood.”

Consider what that instruction required. A lamb killed, and its blood painted on the doorposts of every Israelite house — and every firstborn son in the country would live or die that night on the strength of it. Nothing about blood on a doorframe would strike anyone as protective. Moses had only the word of God that it would work.

“So that the Destroyer of the firstborn might not touch them.” And the Israelites were not exempt by nationality. The angel passed over houses with blood on them, and only those — which is the letter’s whole argument in a single night’s history: not who you are descended from, but whether the blood has been applied.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith the people crossed the Red Sea as on dry land, but the Egyptians, when they attempted to do the same, were drowned. By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days. By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three acts of faith, and the writer has chosen them to make a point about who faith belongs to.

“By faith the people crossed the Red Sea as on dry land, but the Egyptians, when they attempted to do the same, were drowned.”

The same water, the same seabed, the same walls of water on either hand — and two entirely different outcomes. The Egyptians did precisely what Israel did and it killed them.

So the crossing was not a technique. What made the difference was not the action but what stood behind it, exactly as with Abel’s sacrifice in verse 4. This is the chapter’s consistent claim, and carry into any consideration of religious practice: the same act performed by two people is not the same act.

“By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days.”

Here faith takes the form of doing something visibly absurd for a week. An army walking in silence round a fortified city, once a day, watched from the battlements by men who presumably found it very funny by the fourth morning. Nothing happened on days one through six.

That is a detail worth holding on to. Faith frequently looks foolish for a period before it looks like anything at all, and the seventh day is the only one anybody remembers.

“By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient.”

The writer keeps the description. He does not call her the innkeeper or pass over her history, and the placing is deliberate: immediately after Moses and the exodus stands a Canaanite woman of that trade, in the same list, commended on the same terms.

“Because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies.” She had heard what happened at the Red Sea and drew a conclusion the rest of her city refused: the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath (Josh 2:11). She had less evidence than anyone in Jericho and believed more.

Two things follow. She is one of only two women named in this chapter, and she is the only Gentile — and she ended in the genealogy of Christ (Matt 1:5). If the readers of this letter were wondering whether the family of faith was narrowing, the answer is that it always had a Canaanite prostitute in it.

verseByVerse.quote: And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets— who through faith conquered kingdoms, enforced justice, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were made strong out of weakness, became mighty in war, put foreign armies to flight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And what more shall I say? For time would fail me…” The preacher looks at his material and gives up on the attempt to cover it — and the remark is a piece of skill, because the impression of an inexhaustible supply is stronger than another twenty examples would be.

Then six names, and they are not the ones we would have chosen. Gideon, who demanded two signs with a fleece and had to be told his own name for him. Barak, who would not go to battle unless a woman came with him. Samson, whose life was a catalogue of appetite and folly. Jephthah, who made a rash vow with terrible consequences. David, the adulterer and murderer. Samuel, whose sons took bribes.

Not one of them is a model of consistency, and the writer must have known it — his readers knew those stories far better than we do. He puts them in the roll of faith anyway, which tells you what the roll is measuring. Not achievement, and certainly not character. The bare fact of having taken God at his word, in the middle of lives that were often a mess.

Then nine achievements in two verses, rattled off at speed.

“Conquered kingdoms, enforced justice, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions” — Daniel. “Quenched the power of fire” — his three friends. “Escaped the edge of the sword” — David from Saul, Elijah from Jezebel.

“Were made strong out of weakness.” That one deserves its own moment, because it is the pattern of nearly every name on the list. Not strong men who stayed strong. Weak men who were made strong, which is a passive verb and locates the strength somewhere other than in them.

“Became mighty in war, put foreign armies to flight.” The list ends at its most triumphant — and the very next word in the chapter is “women received back their dead”, and then the whole thing turns over.

verseByVerse.quote: Women received back their dead by resurrection. Some were tortured, refusing to accept release, so that they might rise again to a better life. Others suffered mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment. They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were killed with the sword. They went about in skins of sheep and goats, destitute, afflicted, mistreated— of whom the world was not worthy—wandering about in deserts and mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The turn comes mid-verse, and it is the most important structural feature of the chapter.

“Women received back their dead by resurrection” — the widow of Zarephath, the Shunammite. Faith at its most spectacular: a dead child handed back alive.

“Some were tortured, refusing to accept release.”

And with that clause the chapter changes direction entirely. The word for tortured refers to being beaten to death on a rack or frame. “Refusing to accept release” means they were offered a way out and would not take it — the account in 2 Maccabees of the martyrs under Antiochus, which the readers knew well, describes exactly that.

“So that they might rise again to a better life.” Same word as the first clause: resurrection. Some got their dead back by it; some died for it. The identical faith produced both.

Then the catalogue: “mocking and flogging, chains and imprisonment. They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were killed with the sword.” Jewish tradition held that Isaiah was sawn in two under Manasseh; Zechariah was stoned in the temple court (2 Chr 24:21); Jeremiah was imprisoned in a cistern.

“They went about in skins of sheep and goats, destitute, afflicted, mistreated.” This is the prophet’s uniform — Elijah’s hairy cloak — and it is a picture of the men God sent to Israel living like vagrants in the country they were sent to.

Then, in the middle of the squalor, the writer interrupts himself: “of whom the world was not worthy”.

It is the great reversal of the chapter and one of the finest asides in Scripture. The world looked at these people in their goatskins, sleeping in caves, and reckoned them worthless. God’s verdict is that the world was not good enough for them. The judgement ran the other way.

And this is the paragraph the letter’s readers most needed. A congregation whose property had been plundered could look at the first half of the list and wonder why their faith had produced no such deliverance. The second half says: it produced these people too, and God is not ashamed of them either.

verseByVerse.quote: And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised, since God had provided something better for us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised.”

The chapter ends where verse 13 stood: with everybody still waiting. The conquerors and the sawn-in-two, the ones who shut lions’ mouths and the ones the lions ate — all commended, none satisfied.

“Since God had provided something better for us.” And there is the reason, and it is astonishing. They did not receive it because God had something better in view, and the something better involves us.

“That apart from us they should not be made perfect.”

Read that slowly. Abraham cannot be completed without the congregation that first heard this letter read. Moses waits on us. The whole company of the Old Testament faithful is not brought to its end separately and earlier, but together with people who were not born for centuries.

What is the “something better”? Everything the letter has been arguing: the better covenant, the better sacrifice, the better priest. They lived on promises; we live after the fulfilment. They saw the shadow and greeted it from afar; we have the substance.

Which places the readers of this letter in a position they had entirely failed to appreciate. They were drifting back toward the era these giants had lived in and longed to escape — and the whole gallery of them had died waiting for what this discouraged little congregation actually possessed.

“Made perfect” is the letter’s word: brought to completion. And the final note is one of solidarity across the centuries. There is one people of God, not two. Everyone in this chapter and everyone reading it arrives at the same moment, by the same faith, through the same sacrifice — and the writer is about to say what that means for people who are tired: they are not running alone, and the stands are full.

12.title: Fix Your Eyes on Jesus: The Discipline of the Father
12.overview:
Chapter 12 is the pastoral and practical climax of Hebrews. Having presented the great cloud of witnesses in chapter 11, the writer now commands: run. The gallery of faith was not merely historical inspiration; it is the testimony of those who have already finished the race, whose existence is the proof that the race can be completed. Surrounded by this cloud of witnesses, the readers are called to “throw off every weight and the sin that clings so closely” — and run with endurance toward the finish line, with eyes fixed not on the gallery behind them but on Jesus before them.
